articles.title: Why Are Most Union Leaders Silent on Booting Chuck Schumer?
articles.author: Eric Blanc
articles.content: Why have only four national unions publicly backed Chris Van Hollen against Chuck Schumer for Senate leader? The International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers, the Office and Professional Employees International Union, National Nurses United, and the National Union of Healthcare Workers have taken Van Hollen’s side in this urgent fight. But where is everybody else? It’s hard to overstate the stakes. If Democrats once again squander the opportunity given to them by the American people, the lost chance to improve people’s lives — and the ensuing political backlash — could be even worse than what followed the Clinton, Obama, and Biden administrations. Schumer-style corporate politics might as well have been designed in a lab to ensure that Democrats disappoint voters and quickly hand Republicans back the reins of power, perhaps this time under an even more dangerous and effective incarnation of far-right reaction. Missing the Moment There is exactly zero reason to believe Schumer is the man for this moment. He’s a pro-Israel war hawk who is deeply embedded with the same billionaires that Democrats — including every single victorious 2026 Democratic Senate candidate in a battleground state — ran against in these midterms. Want to see the pro-union Protecting the Right to Organize ( PRO) Act and other urgent reforms passed within the first hundred days of the next Democratic administration? So do I. But even if Democrats win the presidency and retain Congress, getting this crucial labor law reform enacted will almost certainly require abolishing the filibuster. Van Hollen has explicitly endorsed doing so. As he put it last Friday , the Senate needs to let majorities govern with “fifty-one votes,” rather than keeping the “antidemocratic” filibuster. Schumer, by contrast, has refused to say whether he’d support getting rid of it. Asked directly after the midterms whether Democrats should abolish the rule, he dodged the question. There’s also plenty a Senate majority leader can do over the next two years, even with Trump still holding the presidential veto. Democrats should aggressively investigate the administration’s corruption and use their control over spending to immediately challenge its worst policies on Iran, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and Israel. Even more important, they’ll need to make crystal clear to Americans the ambitious agenda they’ll enact if they win the White House in 2028. Van Hollen is promising to make the Senate a center of political opposition to billionaire power, putting popular reforms on the table and forcing Republicans to defend their opposition. Schumer is itching to return to the familiar routines of Schumerism: decent policy promises, timid negotiations, and endless excuses for inaction. Plus, he’s insanely unpopular. A November YouGov poll found that just 23 percent of voters viewed Schumer favorably, compared with 39 percent for Trump. That’s right: the Democratic leader most national unions are so far refusing to buck is substantially less popular than Donald Trump. An astonishing 57 percent of voters view Schumer unfavorably. Only 10 percent want him to remain Senate majority leader, compared with 57 percent who want somebody else. Why on earth should the party’s future be placed in the hands of someone so widely disliked? Schumer’s supporters understandably point to the Democratic victories this month. He did help recruit some good candidates, and that deserves some credit. But winning a midterm election amid an unpopular president’s economic and political disasters is a pretty different task from governing successfully afterward. The Case for Van Hollen Like Franklin Delano Roosevelt in the 1930s, Van Hollen comes out of the Democratic establishment but is reading the mood of the public and offering a real alternative to politics as usual. He has called for confronting billionaire power, backed Medicare for All, supported ending the filibuster, and taken a much tougher line on using congressional spending authority to end Trump’s war with Iran. He has also pledged to give the new class of insurgent populist senators a greater role in shaping the party’s direction. Obviously, changing the leader won’t automatically overcome every obstacle to reform. Obviously, switching Senate leaders doesn’t mean the rest of us can sit back and watch the Democrats finally deliver. But there’s a big difference between a leader promising to break with business as usual and one whose career has largely been built around it. Van Hollen has also shown that he’s willing to take political risks for workers. Don’t forget the case of Kilmar Ábrego García, the sheet-metal apprentice and International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail and Transportation Workers (SMART) member who Trump illegally deported to a notorious prison in El Salvador. Van Hollen personally flew there, met with Ábrego García, and helped lead the fight that brought him back to the United States. You would think SMART leadership would back a leader willing to go to such a degree for one of its members. Some national unions have so far made clear that they understand the stakes. The Machinists’ president, Brian Bryant, said Van Hollen understood that the fight was one of “Workers vs. Billionaires.” OPEIU likewise sent Schumer a letter urging him to withdraw and make way for another leader, such as Van Hollen. National Nurses United put the point well in endorsing Van Hollen. Its executive director, Puneet Maharaj, warned that Democrats must not squander the opening voters have given them. Politicking on the K Street Corridor The reason why more national union leaders aren’t yet saying the same isn’t complicated. Many of them feel that a significant part of their job is to build close relationships with congresspeople to deliver for their members and fight for pro-worker legislation. If they back Van Hollen and Schumer wins, there’s a real risk that their union might suddenly find that their calls get returned a little less quickly (or not at all), and that important Democratic leaders might no longer listen to their legislative priorities. That’s a valid concern, especially given how Washington currently works. But it’s also an extraordinarily narrow way to calculate political risk, especially at this moment of crisis. For years now, progressive union leaders have rightly insisted that democracy is on the line, that sky-high economic inequality must be reversed, that the Democrats should stand up for the little guy, and that the labor movement must do everything possible to defeat MAGA and greedy CEOs. Now union leaders and Democrats have a rare opportunity to actually move the needle in that direction. And it wouldn’t even take much effort. This Senate fight is one of those exceedingly rare moments when a union press release could make a historic difference for working people and the country as a whole. There’s no excuse for silence. Schumer is seventy-five and faces reelection in 2028 — if he even chooses to run. He’s hardly a permanent fixture of American politics. And Van Hollen is a respected senator who can work across the party’s ideological divisions. The timidity prevailing on the K Street corridor of downtown DC isn’t an inevitable way of doing politics. Just look at how much bolder unions have been in state-level contests this year. In Michigan, the United Auto Workers (UAW), the American Federation of Teachers (AFT) Michigan, National Nurses United, the Association of Flight Attendants, and United Food and Commercial Workers Local 951 were among the unions that took sides in a fiercely contested Democratic Senate primary, backing Abdul El-Sayed against Schumer’s preferred candidate, Haley Stevens. In Maine, the state AFL-CIO and dozens of local unions went all out for Troy Jackson. And in Minnesota, the Service Employees International Union (SEIU), UNITE HERE Local 17, and others backed Peggy Flanagan against the more establishment-friendly Angie Craig. All three of these Senate winners are now supporting Van Hollen. Moving away from this bold spirit, most national union leaders currently appear to want to stay silent, hoping to square the circle between the evident anger of their base and their desire not to break with Schumer. Some of them have framed the issue to me over the past few days as a matter of fighting for the agenda, not the person. But whether they like it or not, it’s precisely that choice of agenda and strategy that’s now being posed by the Senate leadership fight. Everybody knows that who leads the party has a great deal to do with what the party actually does. It’s a bit disingenuous, too, to suddenly insist that the agenda matters but the leadership doesn’t, given how many national unions came out swinging for Nancy Pelosi when her speakership seemed like it might be challenged in 2018. Back then, the AFL-CIO, AFT, the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, SEIU, UAW, the United Steelworkers, and numerous other unions publicly backed Pelosi in her fight to return as House Speaker. Union leaders understand that the choice of congressional leadership matters for the legislative agenda. Not Too Late My suggestion to rank-and-file members and local and state union leaders is to look at this Van Hollen–Schumer fight as a test of whether their national leaders are ready to meet the moment. If they’re not able to take even this relatively mild risk to help save the Democrats from themselves, why should we expect them to take on the much bigger, even more consequential risks, like backing anti-corporate candidates for office in 2028 or massively investing in new organizing to unionize America afterward? National union leaders still sitting this out or leaning toward Schumer should reconsider. In today’s fight for the future of the Democratic Party, national unions have to choose a side. They can stick with the old, corporate-friendly hacks who helped get us into this mess, or stand with those willing to fight against business as usual. There’s no neutral ground here. articles.title: Labor Mobilized for ‘Many vs. Mighty’ Midterms
articles.author: Jenny Brown
articles.content: Something different was in the air as the labor movement mobilized for the midterms. More than usual, unions were willing to support insurgent candidates who refused corporate donations and bucked the Democratic Party establishment. They championed a Bernie Sanders-style list of working-class issues: Medicare for All, a higher minimum wage, union rights, immigrant rights, stopping war, and taxing the rich. Many are union members themselves. And they won. United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain called the election “the many versus the mighty.” In Michigan, the UAW was a key backer of the victorious Abdul El-Sayed, who earlier defeated the party’s depressing primary choice for U.S. Senate. “You had a lot of rich people who tried to… buy a seat, to buy these races,” Fain told Michigan Advance . “Michiganders… are telling these people they’re not for sale.” Logger and union member Troy Jackson won a Senate seat against 30-year incumbent Republican Susan Collins in Maine after the UAW and the Maine AFL-CIO helped defeat the establishment choice in the primary there. In Ohio, labor stalwart Sherrod Brown faced a river of crypto lobby cash but recovered the Senate seat he lost in 2024. In Texas, the Communications Workers (CWA) mobilized for union-member candidates up and down the ticket, asking candidates to commit to a “Contract with Working Texans.” Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa signed on—she’s a labor lawyer, member of Texas State Employees Union/CWA, and the first Democrat elected Texas governor since 1990. Various union members and leaders are headed for Congress. Ironworker Brian Poindexter won in Ohio. Pennsylvanians elected firefighter and union president Bob Brooks. Forest Service smokejumper and local union vice president Sam Forstag won in Montana. VA nurse and union member Mitchell Berman beat a Republican incumbent in Wisconsin. In New York, UAW members and Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) congressional candidates Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier defeated establishment Democrats in the primary, then romped November 3. Richard Ojeda, a champion of the West Virginia teachers’ strike of 2018, won a Congressional seat in North Carolina, beating the head of the National Republican Congressional Committee. "We were elected to elevate the lives of working people across this country,” said Ojeda . “We're coming in LASER FOCUSED on the mission. Help people. Hold anyone who has hurt people accountable. Tax the billionaires. The end.” Others lost, but came way closer than expected. In Nebraska, Kellogg’s strike leader and independent Dan Osborn came up short (44-50) for U.S. Senate. He faced ferocious attack ads, with $24 million in ‘independent’ spending. In Florida, former SEIU organizer and DSA member Angie Nixon defeated the establishment Democrat in the primary and almost won (48-50) a Senate race the pundits had written off. She got zero support from the national Democratic Party. CORPORATE DEMS UNDER FIRE Now some unions have come out swinging, demanding more from the party. The Machinists (IAM) sent a letter urging Senator Chuck Schumer to resign as party leader . OPEIU did the same . The IAM “is through with any member of leadership, in any political party, who stops one iota short of being a ferocious, unyielding and unbending champion of working people,” said President Brian Bryant. “This means… sweeping economic policy changes that will recalibrate the vast, immoral, economic injustice in this country.” The United Electrical Workers concurred: “The credit for these wins belongs not to the Democratic Party—whose leadership has offered at best tepid resistance to the Republican agenda over the past two years—but to the working people across the country who have spent the last two years organizing and fighting back in their communities and workplaces.” UE set out an ambitious agenda : a $25 minimum wage, Medicare for All, dismantling ICE, taxing the rich, protecting Social Security, and passing labor law reform including the PRO Act and card-check recognition for speedier union recognition. National Nurses United said voters expect a stop to health care cuts, stat. President Trump can veto most bills Congress passes, but Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders insisted on November 9 that Congress needs to do its job and pass a bold working-class agenda. If Trump vetoes the bills, that’ll raise the stakes in 2028 to elect a president who will sign them. It’ll take a lot of pressure get corporate Democrats to defy their paymasters. So plans are afoot for May Day 2028 , when the Auto Workers and other unions have important contracts expiring. The plan is to keep the focus on working class demands, backed by a season of contract campaigns and strikes.

articles.title: ‘Delay, Deny, Discipline’ Is Amazon’s Real Pregnancy Policy, Workers Say
articles.author: Jenny Brown
articles.content: Willamina Barclay was working as a picker at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Rochester, New York, when she felt lightheaded again. “She pleaded with a manager for a seat… He refused: ‘No, because you don’t have a [pregnancy] accommodation. If I give you a chair, I have to give everybody else a chair,’” he said, according to a recent lawsuit. But Barclay, who learned she was pregnant in March 2025, had already asked managers many times for accommodations—a seat, extra breaks to drink, eat, pee (or throw up) in the bathroom, no ladder-climbing or squatting, and no heavy lifting. Amazon—a company known for fast delivery—had failed to answer for weeks, demanding medical documentation. Even after Barclay provided it, Amazon still refused most accommodations, permitting her four breaks a day, but no chair. She was moved to a different position, but still required to lift heavy packages. Amazon counted her new breaks against her unpaid time off (UPT), a leave bank that workers accumulate at five minutes per hour and that maxes out at 80 hours. She went to Human Resources several times to try to rectify the situation, but stopped because they were also counting those visits as UPT, the lawsuit says. The heavy lifting led to sharp pains. At one point she left the warehouse in a wheelchair headed for the hospital. Amazon also counted that time against her unpaid leave bank. On another occasion, she had to leave due to uncontrolled vomiting. Despite a doctor’s note, that was also counted against her. Her UPT thus used up, Amazon fired her. Under the law, workers cannot be penalized for taking pregnancy-related leave (see box at end of article) . Barclay’s ordeal is detailed in a lawsuit filed September 8 by A Better Balance , a nonprofit focused on work policies affecting families. It’s a proposed class action on behalf of all U.S. workers whose rights under the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA) have been violated by Amazon. SYSTEMATIC VIOLATIONS Barclay’s harrowing experience is common, said Sultana Hossain, recording secretary of the Amazon Labor Union (ALU) on Staten Island: Under the law “pregnant workers don’t have to give in paperwork,” she said. “They only have to verbally say, ‘I’m pregnant and I need to be accommodated.’ But we’re seeing Amazon systemically violate that. “Even if workers get an accommodation eventually, it can take several weeks,” said Hossain. “So people really don’t have any choice but to keep working in their regular role, which is really dangerous if they actually need an accommodation.” Key’Asia, a worker at Amazon’s fulfillment center near Wilmington, Delaware, said that Amazon management twice rejected a note from her doctor, once because it had an e-signature, and then again when she got an ink signature. (For privacy to discuss medical matters, some workers asked that last names not be used.) Managers said the signature looked fraudulent and still refused to accommodate her pregnancy, Key’Asia said. “They are making you do the things that your doctor told you that you’re not supposed to be doing,” she told attendees at an online Jobs With Justice event in October. “They’re making you do things that are putting yourself and your baby at risk.” She said Amazon fired her twice, both times when she was pregnant. PATTERN OF ILLEGALITY Workers have noticed a pattern: When they request accommodations, Amazon managers ask if they are “safe to work.” If they say “yes,” they are forced to continue to work without accommodations. If they say “no,” Amazon puts them on unpaid leave , which rapidly runs out. Marissa, who worked at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Rossford, Ohio, said that after her accommodations were denied, she was forced out on unpaid leave, and she ended up losing her apartment. “I was out $1,700… I couldn’t pay for my vehicle. I couldn’t afford to eat. “Amazon doesn’t care about whether or not you’re in pain,” she said. “They care about whether or not you can get their packages out on time.” Hossain said it was typical for workers to get fired for “job abandonment” because “they ran out of time-off options because they were just not given the accommodation.” (A Better Balance has also sued Amazon for this practice on behalf of a disabled worker.) TRAGIC RESULTS Hayat Bzezi was working at Amazon’s Staten Island JFK8 warehouse during the busy holiday season of 2024, when all workers were required to take an additional weekly 10-hour shift. She had asked for lighter duty, and management said she could use a chair, but then she was denied it. She was “lifting heavy products, climbing up and down the stairs, despite having a high-risk pregnancy,” said her husband Wajdy, an elected ALU trustee who works at the same warehouse. Hayat worked through pain, but it got worse and finally she had to go to the hospital, where she miscarried. It was the second time she had miscarried while working at Amazon. After that the couple decided to speak out . Since then, she has stopped working at Amazon and has been able to bear a child. LAW REDUCES MISCARRIAGES When the PWFA went into effect in 2023, a study found that it reduced miscarriages by 9.6 percent. This suggests that many more miscarriages could be avoided if Amazon, the country’s second-largest private employer, started following the law. Pregnant With A Contract Postal workers move packages like Amazon warehouse workers do, but they have a union contract. It makes all the difference when you’re pregnant, said Postal Workers (APWU) national field organizer Lori Cash. She hired into a heavy job at the Postal Service in 1998 while pregnant with her third child. After a couple of months, her doctor told her she needed to stop work, but she had no sick leave or vacation time accrued. “I went to my union steward, and I said, ‘This is what my doctor is telling me, I’m scared.’ I had no idea what my rights were. I’d never been in a union before.” Her steward explained that she could take leave without pay, under the contract, and could not be fired: “We have a just cause process in our contract. They have to prove that they had a just reason to fire you, and just using too much time off without being paid is not justified.” After the birth, Cash came back to work, but it was too hard: “I had two toddlers and a newborn. I was trying to go back to work with all those shenanigans going on at my house with all these babies.” She told her steward she was thinking of quitting. But her steward fought for her to get the option to come back with fewer hours and gradually increase them, which was also guaranteed in their contract. “Pregnancy is stressful,” said Cash. “You have so much to worry about.” But during her next pregnancy, she felt “much more confident that I was going to be able to get the accommodations I needed. I had a whole union behind me, fighting to make sure that those rights were given to me, and to make sure that I had a healthy pregnancy and was able to take the time that I needed for me, and for my baby to be taken care of.” But there is every indication that Amazon is ignoring it. Last year, New Jersey’s attorney general filed a lawsuit against Amazon after reviewing thousands of worker requests for accommodations. Amazon is New Jersey’s largest private employer, with around 50,000 workers. “When Amazon’s pregnant workers and workers with disabilities request accommodations, Amazon stonewalls them,” the suit charges. “It forces them through a byzantine accommodations process, imposing rigid and unnecessary paperwork requirements and subjecting workers to unexplained weeks-long delays.” Rosa, a worker at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Akron, Ohio, said she asked for pregnancy accommodations because she was working in Ship Dock, a role that requires heavy lifting, pushing, and pulling. She was hospitalized for dehydration four times, but managers still kept her in that role, she said. “Eventually my symptoms became so severe that I had to take an unpaid leave of absence,” she said. “I found out afterwards that I could have done paid short-term disability leave, but these options weren’t told to me.” Amazon denies this. “The suggestion that we routinely deny or don’t support pregnancy accommodations is simply untrue,” said Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel. She said “99.9 percent” of pregnancy accommodation requests this year had been approved. But New Jersey investigators found that Amazon regularly fired workers for requesting accommodations, in violation of New Jersey’s Law Against Discrimination and the PWFA. New York State has also sued Amazon for this. Hossain said the medical forms that Amazon requires for pregnancy, injury, and disability accommodations are so comprehensive and invasive that doctors have objected that they violate medical privacy laws. Amazon wants such detailed medical documentation, Hossain said, because “they want to claim that if workers ever get injured, it’s because of conditions they came to work with, and it’s not workplace injuries.” Asked about this, an Amazon public relations representative declined to respond. PACE DRIVES INJURIES The worker justice group Warehouse Life has been tracking and protesting Amazon’s health and safety record since 2023, and helping injured workers who have to “fight through a lot of misinformation and lies that they received from [Amazon] managers about workers’ comp,” said Chloe Sigal, campaign manager for the group. Sigal said Amazon’s rate system, along with “time off task” (TOT) policies, make the work unsafe: “Amazon is pushing people to work as fast, as hard as humanly possible—or really outside what is humanly possible. That’s what’s driving this injury epidemic .” In 2021 the California legislature found that injuries in Amazon warehouses were driven by its rate system. Workers were forced to work faster and faster because if they fell into the lowest 25 percent they could experience discipline, and the bottom 5 percent risked termination. California passed a law requiring warehouses to publish stable quotas and not constantly accelerate them. In 2024 the state fined Amazon $6 million for violating it. Workers also accumulate TOT when surveillance detects a pause in their package scanning. Fear of too much TOT pushes workers to cut short their breaks, skip bathroom breaks (and reduce liquid consumption to match), and push on through pain. Dehydration is particularly risky during a pregnancy. “The reason that people are miscarrying at Amazon is because of this rate system,” said Sigal. Doctors agree. Jenny Fish is a Santa Rosa, California, physician who provides prenatal care. “Prolonged standing, going the whole shift without water, lifting more than 15 to 20 pounds, working night shifts regularly,” she said, “all of this has been irrefutably linked to higher risk of miscarriage, preeclampsia, increased maternal fatigue, preterm delivery, low birth weight, and just in general adverse birth outcomes.” Preeclampsia is potentially fatal. IS THERE A POLICY? Sigal said that soon after Warehouse Life started, several Amazon workers came to the group reporting pregnancy issues. But when the group put out a call on social media for experiences working at Amazon while pregnant, it was flooded with stories. Two thousand women from 40 states responded, and 81 described loss of a pregnancy. (To talk to Warehouse Life, schedule a call here .) Now some of these workers are leading the charge to get changes at the company. They have put pressure on New York City’s Mt. Sinai Health System to terminate Amazon Board of Directors member Edith Cooper as a hospital trustee, given Amazon’s dismal safety record. Warehouse Life members have also met with Amazon management. Sigal said that during those meetings Amazon claimed to have a policy on pregnancy that was only available to workers. But no workers were able to access it. “Nobody has it. We’ve heard from managers that they don’t have it either, that they don’t receive training on what to do,” Sigal said. When Labor Notes asked Amazon for its pregnancy policy and any training materials, no documents were forthcoming. Warehouse Life counters that the company’s real pregnancy policy is “Delay. Deny. Discipline.” MARCH ON H.R. The Amazon Labor Union organized on Staten Island in 2022, and in 2024 affiliated with the Teamsters. But Amazon refuses to negotiate with the union at the 5,000-worker warehouse, despite being ordered to do so by the National Labor Relations Board in April. The union can still help, though. “Just a few weeks ago a pregnant worker came to our union hall saying she wanted help getting an accommodation at work,” said ALU’s Hossain. The worker had already told her manager that she was pregnant. The union sent several workers to accompany her to H.R., saying “that should be enough, and Amazon needs to start the process of accommodating her,” Hossain said. “And they actually did listen, but only because a group of workers accompanied her.” A contract could provide additional protections (see box at upper right) . The union isn’t waiting for workers to seek it out. Union activists distribute fliers with a QR code to a reporting form that goes to the union. Half of the reports “are unfair discipline, the other half is workers who are dealing with injuries or the accommodation process or need workers’ comp or whatever,” said Hossain. “It’s such a big issue.” “It really does feel like we’re all just numbers,” said Rosa in Akron. “I want them to take more accountability. They make it so hard when it comes to a life-changing thing.” Pregnancy Rights It has been illegal to discriminate against pregnant workers since 1978, when feminist agitation won the Pregnancy Discrimination Act (under Title VII of the 1964 Civil Rights Act), which says employers can’t discriminate based on pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions. Before that, many employers had a policy of terminating workers when they got pregnant, and pregnant women often weren’t eligible for unemployment insurance. In 2023, the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act strengthened pregnancy rights. Now employers are required to make reasonable accommodations. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has found that reasonable accommodations which don’t require a doctor’s note include: a seat; additional breaks to eat, drink, or use the bathroom; adjusted uniforms and safety equipment; and changes to your job duties or your schedule to make it possible for you to keep working safely while you’re pregnant or recovering from a birth. Additional accommodations that might require a doctor’s note include limits on weight you have to lift, bending, and ladder use. “But you still have the right to get those accommodations quickly and have them implemented effectively,” said Katherine Greenberg, attorney with A Better Balance . “It is illegal for employers like Amazon to force workers to take a leave of absence if there’s an on-the-job accommodation that would keep them safe and allow them to keep working and earning an income,” said Greenberg. Also, employers can’t punish workers for asking for or needing accommodations. “If you need to pump milk for your baby, you have the right to take a lactation break without being punished for too much time off task,” said Greenberg. “Or if you experience a miscarriage and you need to miss work to recover, you have the right to take that time without being deducted UPT or assigned points for your absence.” Your state or city may have additional protections; check here . Have a question or concern about your pregnancy at Amazon? Schedule a call with Warehouse Life here .

articles.title: The American Woman Who Joined Algeria’s Socialist Experiment
articles.author: Julia Harte
articles.content: Within days of arriving in Algeria, months after its liberation from France in 1962, Elaine Klein knew she was there for the long haul. “The experiment to create a new socialist country from the impoverished colony, the tremendous task of building a state respected in the international arena, was daunting,” she later wrote. Yet, “My gut told me that I would settle here.” Her intuition was correct. For more than a decade, the Jewish New Yorker was the only American in Algeria’s new government. She assumed a range of roles — reporter, translator, envoy — as the former French colony established itself as an international haven for resistance groups, political dissidents, and anti-colonial organizers. Klein was not the only one taking on new responsibilities. A national program of popular self-management, or “autogestion,” was implemented soon after the revolution, giving the Algerian people ownership of the farms, businesses, and buildings abandoned by fleeing European settlers. A coup led by military chief Houari Boumédiène overthrew the first postcolonial government. The autogestion experiment largely ended, though Boumédiène kept trying to close Algeria’s wealth gap and resist economic subordination by the Global North. Klein also continued to cover progressive and socialist assemblages around the world on behalf of the national press agency, Algérie Presse Service. When the Organization of Latin American Solidarity gathered in Cuba in 1967 to form a united front against US imperialism, she attended a press conference where Stokely Carmichael called “white Western imperialist society” the “common enemy” of all the delegates present and declared, “Our struggle is to overthrow this system which feeds itself and expands itself through the economic and cultural exploitation of nonwhite, non-Western peoples.” Klein took the opportunity to invite Carmichael to visit Algeria later that year: his first trip to the African continent. Into the early 1970s, she served as a sort of domestic ambassador for other Black Panthers and leaders of international revolutionary movements who flocked to open offices in Algiers, a city dubbed the “Mecca of Revolution” by Pan-African Bissau-Guinean poet Amílcar Cabral and the “third world capital” by Klein. Her work brought her under the scope of a vast CIA operation aimed at uncovering foreign involvement in domestic protest movements within the United States. The FBI’s COINTELPRO initiative helped drive a wedge between the international wing of the Black Panther Party, which Klein helped establish, and their US-based counterparts. After more than a decade in Algeria, Klein herself was forced to leave when she refused to spy on a friend for the Boumédiène regime. Her idealism, however, never wavered. Until her death this September, she followed an irrepressible impulse to stand with other humans fighting for freedom and self-government, no matter where they were. And despite the remarkable role she played in some of the twentieth century’s most historic anti-colonial, social ownership, and civil rights movements, she never thought of herself as anything more or less than a world citizen. Revolution in the Third World Klein first encountered the Algerian anti-colonial movement at the 1952 May Day parade in Paris. She had moved to France months earlier, after being pushed out of her job in New York with the United World Federalists (UWF). The UWF, part of an emerging “world government” movement that aimed to eradicate war and establish a system of global justice, had fractured due to internal divisions and external pressure from US authorities, a process that would recur with many causes Klein championed over time. After moving to Paris, she began learning the history of decoloni­zation in North and West Africa through work as a French–English conference interpreter. In 1960, the year that eleven African countries — including nine former French colonies — became independent, she helped organize a congress in Ghana, the first African state to shake off colonial rule. There she developed a fast friendship with Frantz Fanon, whom the Algerian provisional government had recently named their ambassador to Ghana. Back in New York later that year, Klein met the Algerian provisional government’s representative to the United Nations. He hired her on the spot to write promotional material and lobby for Algerian independence at the United Nations. On December 19, 1960, those efforts would pay off when the General Assembly voted 63–8 to recognize Algeria’s right to self-rule. (The United States and twenty-seven other countries abstained.) As Mokhtefi later told me, the unexpected job was a long-awaited opportunity for “digging in” and “getting my hands dirty” in the decolonization cause that she had long supported. When France recognized Algerian independence in the summer of 1962, a brief power struggle ensued inside the National Liberation Front, the party that had led Algeria’s revolution. One of the Front’s original leaders, Ahmed Ben Bella, and Boumédiène, the head of his army, took control of Algiers in September. Klein arrived in October and started working for the tourism authority, a largely theoretical job in a country that would receive no tourists for years to come. Upon learning she was from New York, Ben Bella’s press and information adviser hired her as his assistant. From there, she was transferred to the government’s secretary general, an office that produced agendas, reports, and press releases for meetings of Algeria’s cabinet. Finally, she was moved to Algérie Presse Service, where she wrote daily op-eds and became the entire “English desk.” Ben Bella was an outspoken adherent of Third Worldism, the anti-imperialist, anti-racist movement through which current and former colonies united to resist oppression by European powers as well as, eventually, the American and Sino-Soviet blocs during the Cold War. Third Worldists, as political scientist Robert Malley put it, had an “uneasy coexistence” with the Eurocentrism and cultural superiority embedded in some Marxist theory; Friedrich Engels in 1848 had described France’s conquest of Algeria as “an important and fortunate fact for the progress of civilization.” Yet following the 1962 exodus of French colonists, or “pieds noirs,” socialists from around the world flocked to Algeria, drawn by the revolutionaries’ vision of a more democratic, egalitarian state. These foreigners would become known as “pieds rouges” after Ben Bella’s overthrow ousted many of them from Algeria too. Among them was the Greek Trotskyist Michalis Raptis, aka Michel Pablo. While leading the Fourth International during the 1950s, Pablo had devised a counterfeit-money scheme to buy weapons for Algerian revolutionaries on the world market and had established an arms factory for them in Morocco. Soon after Pablo arrived in independent Algeria, he became an economic adviser to Ben Bella, presiding over the campaign of “autogestion” that put the nation’s resources under popular control. Modeled on similar experiments in Cuba and Yugoslavia — countries that also sent medical teams to Algeria to help replace the European health care personnel who had fled — Algeria’s self-management program established worker-run committees to oversee the farms, industrial enterprises, and estates left behind by the colonial regime. After attending an Algerian congress on industrial self-management in 1964, the Trotskyist French militant Daniel Guérin wrote that the event had been “dominated” by the emergence of “a working class, of a socialist awareness.” Ben Bella himself embraced socialism at public rallies and within his government, opening a National Office for the Support of the Socialist Sector. This enthusiasm was short-lived, however. Ben Bella’s other advisers persuaded him to fold the socialist sector support office into the agricultural ministry and to exert more central control over the self-managed farms, giving rise to a corrupt bureaucracy. While the National Liberation Front continued to publicly tout Algeria as a self-managed socialist state, the country slipped further from that ideal. “Power and increasing adulation isolated [Ben Bella] from a truthful examination of events,” according to Klein. “He launched new national projects every day, but neglected the measures required to implement them; he created offices and agencies that functioned in name only.” Ben Bella also began to take more punitive measures against domestic dissidents, arresting, torturing and banishing those who criticized him. Three years after Algeria had won its independence, Boumédiène led a coup in which Ben Bella was arrested. It was the result of an internal power struggle more than an ideological rift; Boumédiène would continue to pursue some of the same progressive social policies and redistribution measures as his predecessor. But many pieds rouges, including Pablo, were branded foreign atheists and forced out of Algeria. Klein stayed, even though she had joined popular protests against the coup. Her fluency in English and French — a rare combination in postrevolutionary Algeria — had made her useful to the foreign affairs minister, Abdelaziz Bouteflika, a key ally of Boumédiène. “Hope remained that one day everything would be put right,” Klein later wrote. “And we all went back to work.” Panthers, Trotskyists, and G-Men In the summer of 1969, two years after she had invited Carmichael to Algeria and shown him around the country, Klein received a call that another Black Panther leader was in Algiers — and needed her help establishing a permanent presence there. Eldridge Cleaver had fled the United States several months earlier after exchanging shots with Oakland police the night of Martin Luther King Jr’s assassination. For Klein, who had protested racial segregation in the United States since college and reported on the rise of the Black Panther Party for the Algerian press, the opportunity to work for the Panthers was thrilling. As with many in the Third Worldist movement, she saw anti-racist and anti-colonial activism as inseparable. Klein helped formalize Cleaver’s status in the country by involving him in the world’s first Pan-African Cultural Festival, which she organized in Algiers soon after his arrival. She also helped Cleaver and other Panthers establish the party’s international branch there, and accompanied his wife Kathleen on a speaking tour back in the United States. As Cleaver settled into Algeria, he took a more militantly anti-American stance and strengthened the Panthers’ Third World, anti-colonial bona fides through new alliances with figures such as North Korea’s Kim Il Sung and the Palestinian Fatah leader Yasser Arafat. In a 1971 interview with a San Francisco radio station, Cleaver proudly claimed that Black Panther members serving in Vietnam had switched sides, fighting against the US war effort there. These moves clashed with the priorities of the US-based Panthers, who, depleted of personnel and funds by the number of Panthers who had ended up in prison, were trying to put more resources into peace­ful community service programs. In March 1970, as part of its COINTELPRO effort to “expose, disrupt, misdirect, discredit, or otherwise neutralize the activities of black nationalist, hate-type organizations and groupings,” the FBI’s second most powerful official recom­mended that the Bureau send Cleaver a letter “aimed at inflaming the dispute” by telling Cleaver he was being undercut by US-based Black Panther Party leaders. One year later, as Cleaver was on the brink of completely falling out with one such leader, Huey Newton, J. Edgar Hoover endorsed a plan to send Cleaver and Newton spurious correspondence designed to “provoke the existing difficulty” between them. One fake letter purported to show Newton denouncing Cleaver to Boumédiène. Ten­sions between the Algerian government and the Black Panthers, meanwhile, had been building, exacerbated by the Panthers’ disinclination to inte­grate into Algerian society. There was also a fundamental contradiction between the goals of the Algiers-based Panthers and those of the Algerian government. For Cleaver, the Black Panther Party had a singular objective: overthrowing the US government. But Algerian leaders wanted to limit their military aid to freedom fighters trying to liberate their countries from foreign colonization. The mutual frustration between the Algerian authorities and their American guests peaked in August 1972. That month, members of the Black Lib­eration Army, a splinter group started by former Black Panthers who had rejected Huey Newton as too moderate, hijacked a Delta flight from Detroit destined for Miami and landed it in Algiers. They planned to donate their $1 million ransom from the airline to the international Black Panthers, but Algerian authorities confiscated the funds and returned them to Delta. When Cleaver demanded the money, local police raided the Panther villa and took their weapons. Cleaver was never officially deported, but with other Panthers also leaving Algiers, he decided to leave. To extract Cleaver from Algeria, Klein enlisted the help of none other than Michel Pablo, who had fled to France after Boumédiène’s 1965 coup. The former Fourth International secretary and Ben Bella adviser who had once counterfeited money to supply arms to Algeria’s revolutionary army sprang into action once more to help a different kind of revolutionary leave Algeria. Pablo gave Klein the number of a “passer” who could meet Cleaver at the Geneva airport and covertly drive him over the border into France. Pablo also supplied her with a “classy British passport with a photo of a Black man who could have been a younger Eldridge,” as Klein wrote in her memoir. She arranged a safe house for Cleaver and helped him find French lawyers to petition for his asylum there. Klein’s own position in Algeria was becoming more precarious under Boumédiène’s regime. In 1972, secu­rity agents asked her to spy on a friend of hers who had married Ben Bella, and she refused. Two years later, Klein herself was forced into exile from the country to which she had devoted her life. But she had a companion by her side. Two years earlier, a mutual friend had set her up with Mokhtar Mokhtefi: a dashing hero of the Algerian Revolution, who was also rapidly grow­ing disillusioned with the authoritarian turn of the post-independence lead­ership. When Mokhtefi ended up in France, Mokhtar followed, and they lived there for two decades, doing a mix of odd jobs — from making jewelry to writing children’s books — before moving to the United States in 1994. As she forged a new life first in Paris and ultimately in New York City, Algeria underwent its own identity crises and political convulsions, straying even farther from the socialist ambitions that had defined its early years of independence. When Bouteflika — the Boumédiène-aligned foreign affairs minister who had used Klein’s translation services in the 1960s — became president of Algeria in 1999, he shored up his power by enriching a small group of oligarchs at the expense of the general population. Twenty years into his presidency, Bouteflika was forced out of office by the largest popular opposition movement in Algeria since the revolution that had launched his political career sixty years earlier. On November 1, 2019, the sixty-fifth anniversary of the start of the revolution, tens of thousands of demonstrators who called themselves the Hirak (Arabic for “movement”) surged through Algiers to protest Bouteflika’s final efforts to cling to power. “Algeria will take back its independence,” they chanted in Arabic, clapping in time to the syncopated rallying cry. Young and old Algerians waved flags as they marched in the streets or banged on pots and pans from their windows in solidarity. Among the protesters thronging the main streets of Algiers so densely that it was almost impossible to move, Elaine Klein — now Elaine Mokhtefi and ninety years old — could be seen in the crowd, glowing with excitement and cheering on the Hirak with the slogans of the new revolutionaries. “I’ve Started to Talk, and I Don’t Stop” I first visited Mokhtefi at her Manhattan apartment in 2021, when I emailed her out of the blue to ask if I could interview her for a book I was writing about Americans who had traveled abroad to join revolutionary liberation movements. We spoke for several hours about the remarkable trajectory of her life and the causes she and Mokhtar continued to support after moving back to the United States. It was a lonely repatriation for Mokhtefi, at first: “There was nobody to tell what had happened, neither about the Black Panthers, nor about the Algerian war. Everyone seemed very far from all that.” But she and Mokhtar were not idle. “We had to contribute,” she said. “We had to show that we were still responsible world citizens.” They joined Palestinian liberation demonstrations, climate justice marches, and visited encamped protesters at Zuccotti Park several times during the 2011 Occupy Wall Street movement. Elaine Mokhtefi, date unknown. (Dzkouslavia / CC BY-SA 3.0 ) Mokhtar died in 2015, forty-three years after he and Mokhtefi first met. Writing her memoir, Algiers, Third World Capital: Freedom Fighters, Revolutionaries, Black Panthers , Mokhtefi told me, had saved her from a pit of grief that she feared might swallow her up. But ever since it was published in 2018, “and I went on these tours, and I saw that people were really inter­ested in what I had lived,” she continued, “I’ve started to talk, and I don’t stop.” I stayed in touch with Mokhtefi as I continued working on my chapter about her. In 2022, I went to Algiers to visit prominent sites from her time there and interview former Algerian revolutionaries whose paths had crossed with hers. Eventually she met my partner and daughter, and I got to know many of her friends. Every time we saw each other, I marveled at how busy her social life and traveling schedule remained, even as she grew frailer and memories eluded her more often. In August, I visited her apartment one last time to attend a party she threw to celebrate receiving Algerian nationality in recognition of her service to the nation. By then, I had a copy of my own book to give her. A few weeks later — three days before her sudden death — she emailed me, telling me she had started reading my book from the beginning, but that about halfway through the second chapter, “I couldn’t hold myself back, I had to read about me. I just wasn’t capable of waiting my turn. What an experience . . . Thanks, merci, gracias, saha as the Algerians say, the works. I felt so full of myself, validated well beyond any merit.” She told me how lucky she felt that we had entered each other’s lives. Then she added, “I will read the other chapters and see your perspective through to the end, and with such pleasure. With love, Elaine.” This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Iran Dirty Bomb Allegations
articles.author: William J. Astore
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. I woke to the news that America’s mainstream media , always judicious and careful, sees a profound threat from Iran: A dirty bomb to be used against Washington, DC. Sources? Anonymous. Does Iran truly have a bomb or even the capability to deploy it against DC? Unlikely. Truth doesn’t matter here. It’s all about countering momentum building in Congress to put an end to the Iran war. Aaron Maté puts it well in this tweet: The Trump admin committed an unprecedented faux pas before launching its war on Iran: it didn't bother feeding corporate media a pro-war lie to promote. With one "dirty bomb" leak, harmony is being restored to the Beltway propaganda system: https://t.co/19E1KjLOWk — Aaron Maté (@aaronjmate) November 17, 2026 From 2002-03, we all remember the false allegation that Iraq had WMD and that Saddam Hussein was ready to use the same against America. As the saying went back then, “We can’t allow the smoking gun to become a mushroom cloud.” So the Bush/Cheney administration launched the disastrous Iraq war to destroy WMD that Iraq didn’t possess. Back to Iran. After declaring that he’d already destroyed alleged Iranian efforts to build a nuclear bomb, President Trump pivoted to say the Iran war is now about preventing Iran from building a nuke. That contradiction was so obvious, that rationale has proven to be so unpersuasive, that a new one had to be deployed, hence new allegations of a “dirty bomb,” which is in theory easier to make. Now, why Iran would attack DC with a dirty bomb, knowing that U.S. warmongers would likely respond by nuking Tehran, is anyone’s guess. I suppose Trump would respond that Iranians are terrorists and maniacs whose actions make no sense—to that, as we used to say, “it takes one to know one.” Related: Schumer and Jeffries: The Known Unknowns Sadly, the “Blunami” two weeks ago is unlikely to change Washington’s warmongering. While some Democrats may wish to block funding in Congress for the Iran war, they are unlikely to succeed, given Hakeem Jeffries, a tool of Israel, as Speaker. The old “Iraq has WMD!” ploy is being revived to cow Democrats into continuing to support the Iran war. After all, who wants to be blamed, even rhetorically, for allowing Iran to march a dirty bomb through Trump’s imaginary triumphant arch in DC? Addendum: It appears Democrats are preparing a $15 billion war aid package for Ukraine while criticizing Trump for being insufficiently hawkish on Russia and China. Something tells me the Pentagon budget is safe from major cuts. Or any cuts.

articles.title: Russell Vought Federal Grant Plan
articles.author: Marcus Baram
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Kandy Fatheree runs the Summit County Sheriff’s Office in Ohio’s fourth-largest county. Randall Longenecker spent 30 years as a rural family doctor — delivering babies in small-town practice, then training a generation of physicians to do the same. The National Small Business Association has been a nonpartisan voice in Washington for nearly nine decades. None of them are the usual suspects in a fight with the administration of President Donald Trump. Yet all three filed formal objections to a proposed rule by the White House’s Office of Management and Budget that would hand political appointees sweeping authority over hundreds of billions of dollars a year in federal grants. In doing so, they joined opponents who range from county commissioners in Idaho to domestic violence advocates in New York City to a self-described free-market conservative at George Mason University, as well as community groups, nonprofits and foundations across the country. “Although I am sympathetic to the stated intention of this rule, I predict the consequences will be just the opposite of those intended,” Longenecker said in a comment to OMB in July, adding: “The unhealthy changes are so pervasive, I don’t know where to start.” The proposal would rewrite the rulebook governing how federal grants and cooperative agreements — such as funds for scientific research; broadband internet infrastructure; and state, local and tribal assistance — are awarded, managed and terminated. Senior political appointees would review them for alignment with administration priorities and executive orders, with final say over peer reviewers. Currently, such decisions go through a merit-based peer review process involving independent panels of nonpartisan scientists, clinicians, engineers and subject matter experts. But under the proposed overhaul, appointees could terminate any award, including active multiyear grants, if it no longer served “program goals, Federal agency priorities or the national interest.” That change worries Alex Tabarrok, a professor of economics at George Mason University, who was blunt in his critique of the proposal in a blog post last spring : “Political review of every award, peer review demoted, agency review promoted, termination whenever ‘priorities’ change. Chilling.” He called it “a nightmare of petty low-trust review of the kind that is already drowning science.” Related: Starbucks Gets a Tax Break: Families Pick Up the Tab The Office of Management and Budget — which plays a central role in implementing the president’s policy vision, management priorities and spending plans — said that the rule will bar grants from being used to “fund, promote, encourage, subsidize, or facilitate” diversity, equity, inclusion and accessibility and for “government sponsorship of gender ideology and other radical doctrines” and what the administration calls “child sexual mutilation,” its term for gender-affirming care. The proposal also prohibits using federal grant funding for voter registration, issue advocacy or political activity. The proposed rule, which was scheduled to take effect Oct. 1, drew close to 500,000 public comments, with reportedly 95% of them in opposition to the overhaul . Congress postponed its implementation to Dec.11 through the stopgap spending bill Trump signed in September. And the new Democratic-controlled Congress that takes office in January could stop or block the proposal through the appropriations process by explicitly barring the use of federal funds to develop, finalize, implement or enforce the rule. The White House and OMB did not respond to Capital & Main’s requests for comment. Supporters said the rule would impose needed discipline. Among them is the Heritage Foundation, whose Project 2025 document was written by current OMB head Russell Vought and which advocated for expanding executive power and reducing the independence of career civil servants and peer review processes. The conservative think tank has voiced support for the proposal’s DEI and gender-related restrictions and praised the proposal for establishing a single “control tower” to execute the administration’s agenda. Fiscal watchdog groups focused on immigration-related mandates and tighter payment controls against waste and fraud. The coalition opposing the proposal spans major universities, scientific and medical research institutions, civil liberties groups, local governments, nonprofits, law enforcement agencies and both Democratic and Republican lawmakers. Critics argued that the rule would fundamentally damage American innovation and public welfare by replacing the objective system of scientific peer review with political litmus tests administered by executive branch appointees. Opponents also said that the proposal unlawfully usurps Congress’s constitutional power to authorize federal spending. Serving and Protecting Fatheree’s Summit County Sheriff’s Office relies on federal grants for jail operations, mental health and substance abuse treatment, gun violence reduction, and narcotics and human trafficking cases, she said in a comment to OMB in July. Fluctuating requirements would burden agencies that “already face staffing shortages and limited administrative capacity,” she said, and letting agencies terminate funding “based on political considerations and policy priorities unrelated to the recipient’s actual performance undermines responsible long-term planning and introduces instability into otherwise reliable grant programs that have historically and consistently demonstrated positive public safety outcomes.” The Vera Institute of Justice, a nonprofit that focuses on immigration and criminal justice reform, flagged what it called a deeper vulnerability. The Community Oriented Policing Services, or COPS, program, which funds local police hiring, now exists only through annual appropriations rather than an underlying statute. “Ironically, considering the administration’s frequent statements of support for police and the DOJ’s $300 million Model Cities Initiative to ‘supercharge’ law enforcement, the new rule would place COPS funding—and the local law enforcement agencies that depend on it—in the same precarious position as discretionary grants for legal aid or violence intervention,” said Sam Feineh, Vera’s senior advocacy strategist , in a comment submitted to the OMB. Related: Trump's Coal Revival Is Raising Electric Bills—and Voters Are Fighting Back Cooperation Becomes Coercion Longenecker, a retired assistant dean emeritus of Ohio University Heritage College of Osteopathic Medicine who now lives in Bridgewater, Virginia, began applying for and implementing federal rural medical education grants through the federal Health Resources and Services Administration in 2010. The most recent grant he oversaw, to fund a technical assistance center for rural residency programs, has been successful, he said in an interview, but has become “increasingly difficult to work with because of so many layers of approval. Cooperation has become a coercion.” Colleagues still in grant leadership are “fearful of having a target on their back for anything they say.” “I experienced the same kind of micromanagement under multiple administrations,” Longenecker said. “The proposed way of managing grants would make it 10 times worse.” Rural programs, he added, are “the last mile” of a system of rules written by people “that have no clue how it actually works on the ground.” Michelle Salvaggio, an infectious disease specialist at the University of Oklahoma College of Medicine, said that local health departments depend on pass-through funding for disease surveillance, outbreak investigations and immunization programs. “During an outbreak or other public health emergency, a lack of reliable funding and the threat of grant termination without warning could cost lives by delaying detection, response and treatment efforts,” she said in a comment to OMB. The National Small Business Association, with more than 65,000 members, told OMB in a July letter that small firms “depend on a measure of predictability in their relationship with the federal government that this rule, however well-intentioned, would put at risk.” For a business that has hired staff, signed a lease or committed to subcontractors on the strength of a multiyear award, the group said, “that is a significant and largely uninsurable risk.” The Midnight Email The rule’s reach would extend beyond research grants. A provision allowing agencies to change the terms and conditions of awards after work has begun could touch some of the $900 billion a year in grants that flow to state and local governments, according to the Center for Budget and Policy Priorities . In New Jersey, roughly 30% of the state budget comes from Washington, and much of what towns receive as state money started out as federal money, Melinda Rostal, an epidemiologist with the national volunteer group Defend Public Health , told Capital & Main. “They said we can’t run the town without federal funding,” she said of her own town council in Weehawken, New Jersey. Safe Horizon, a nonprofit that supports crime survivors across New York City, draws about 25% of its funding from federal dollars, Liz Roberts, CEO of Safe Horizon, told Capital & Main. It has already walked away from one grant — a federal Office on Violence Against Women award that required a certification committing the group to treat domestic violence “only as a crime” and to recognize “that there are only two sexes.” Those requirements were later struck down by a federal court . Related: GOP Candidate Exploits Data Center Backlash to Hit Solar, Wind in Wisconsin Declining the grant in 2025 cost the organization about $1 million a year and pulled advocates providing legal assistance from the Bronx Criminal Court, where the group has had a daily presence for decades, Roberts said. On Feb. 6, Roberts said, the group received an email at midnight which she explained stated that another grant for substance abuse and mental health services was “cut off effective immediately.” Forty-eight hours later, amid political pushback, the government reversed itself. “It would have taken services away from traumatized children,” Roberts said. The larger threat, she added, is pass-through money. New York City funds about 65% of the budget for its domestic violence shelters with federal money from the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program. If those funds were to be cut off under the proposed rule change, Roberts said, “it could literally result in us having to shut down our domestic violence shelters.” Safe Horizon runs and operates eight of them throughout the city, housing about 800 people a night. Political Litmus Test Elizabeth M. Ginexi, a former National Institutes of Health scientific program official, said that the rule would impose a “new political litmus test” on federal grants — an “impossible conflict” for organizations whose clients “are, by definition, the ones equity-focused programs are designed to reach.” As an example of funding that could be in jeopardy, she cited a drug crisis intervention grant in a rural Maine county of generational fishing families that reported a high number of LGBTQ youth. The Maine Center for Economic Policy, a nonpartisan research organization, estimated the rule could put roughly $6 billion in federal funding to the state at risk. Rostal with Defend Public Health argued that the rule is an attempt to legalize what courts have blocked. Courts restored many early grant terminations at the start of the Trump administration in 2025 because agencies skipped required procedures, she said. “So now they’re going a step further and they’re changing the actual administrative procedures to make it legal,” she said. Related: Arizona’s Rising Electric Bills Are Reshaping the 2026 Midterms Rostal said that oversteps the executive branch’s authority. “It’s not the president’s job to decide whether or not we’re helping inner city kids or whether or not we’re maintaining rural hospitals,” she said. “That’s Congress’ decision.” Longenecker said he usually tries to offer agencies constructive tweaks. This time he came up empty. “I can’t even give a little piece of advice,” he said, “except to say this whole thing is so pervasively messed up that it just isn’t going to work.” Capital & Main

articles.title: The Longest Hotel Strike in Washington State History
articles.author: Diana Varenik
articles.content: You’d be forgiven for worrying, twelve weeks into a strike, that the boss is hell-bent on waiting you out. But after more than eighty days on the picket line at Seattle’s Embassy Suites by Hilton in Pioneer Square, Aspen Desmarais was undeterred. “I can live on a budget,” she said. “Been doing it since day one.” After eighty-five days, on September 10, workers won the longest hotel strike in Washington state history. Their union, UNITE HERE Local 8, represents four thousand hospitality workers in Oregon and Washington. Desmarais, a strike captain and bartender at the hotel, worked to keep others motivated throughout the fight. She and her coworkers were “tired of people talking down to us and not treating us with respect,” she said, “when we’re the reason that place stays running the way that it does.” Hilton’s offer, two weeks into the strike, of one cent per hour over its previous proposal helped fuel outrage. The union held open bargaining, so members heard the offer firsthand. “I [felt] frustrated and disrespected,” Desmarais said. “Especially with how much hard work my coworkers put into making sure the hotel and its guests have clean spaces and stays that are welcoming.” Fritzie Corral, an Embassy Suites breakfast attendant, had only worked at the hotel for two months before walking out. As the strike went on, she said, her son worried that she had made a mistake in taking the job. “You see other employees that decided to stay in the hotel working,” she said. “Even during that time, I still believed I made the right choice. It’s my right to voice out what I feel and to fight for my rights.” Hilton did not respond to requests for comment. Protection From ICE Workers won significant pay increases, lowered barriers for health care eligibility, and highly sought-after protections for immigrant workers. Hilton, which manages the hotel, drew protests earlier this year for housing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents and for cutting ties with a Minneapolis hotel that canceled ICE bookings during Operation Metro Surge. The union’s leaders criticized Hilton throughout the strike for dismissing contract language that would protect immigrant workers. “With ICE-related killings in the news for months causing immigrant workers to worry, why is Hilton refusing to give immigrant workers’ union a heads up if ICE is staying at the hotel?” Local 8 President Anita Seth asked Business Wire . Ultimately workers won a commitment from Hilton not to punish workers who call out due to an immigration enforcement surge, plus language binding the hotel to an expedited resolution process in such an event. Workers who lose their work authorization due to immigration enforcement will now be able to return to their jobs if their work authorization is restored within four years, and to retain their seniority for up to two. Desmarais told Labor Notes that making sure immigrant coworkers missing work because of ICE “knew they would have a job still and a safe place to come back to” was the “most important” win strikers fought for. Starting in 2027, housekeepers will make over $31 an hour — a giant step above the $17.63 an hour that housekeepers make on average across the country, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The new contract makes them the highest-paid housekeepers in the state, according to the union. Embassy Suites workers classified as “tipped” will now make $1 more per hour than the city’s minimum wage. Health care eligibility was also a core demand for the union. Many hotel workers under collective bargaining agreements must meet a minimum threshold of hours worked to qualify for health benefits in a given period. Seasonal layoffs, a hallmark of hotel work, often mean inconsistent coverage for workers and their families. The new contract replaces the month-to-month eligibility standard with an annual threshold of 1,250 hours, or around twenty-four hours a week, to qualify. Mass Cancellations The strike coincided with five of the six World Cup soccer matches held at Seattle’s Lumen Field this summer, directly across from the Embassy Suites. World Cup–related leverage helped produce quick contract wins this summer for service and hospitality workers in Philadelphia, New York, and Los Angeles, but not so in Seattle. How did strikers there keep up the pressure for another sixty-three days after the games ended? The hotel’s proximity to Lumen Field makes it a destination for football fans when the season starts in September. On game days, the hotel sets up a bar facing the stadium. Workers set up a separate picket line mere feet away from the customers and urged fans not to cross. In between sporting events, Desmarais said solidarity from other union workers played a big role. Combined pressure from Burlington Northern Santa Fe Railway (BNSF) railworkers (represented by the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen Division 518) and sympathetic elected officials pushed Sound Transit to move its contract to another hotel with no promise of return. The transit agency had maintained a block of rooms for the BNSF workers who operate its commuter rail — accounting for twenty-five rooms nightly, or roughly $18,500 in weekly revenues, according to Local 8, and a significant portion of the hotel’s income during low-traffic winter months. Embassy Suites workers like Desmarais worked hard to push Sound Transit and other hotel clients to honor the picket line. “There was one day I had to make over ninety phone calls,” she said. “For the most part, it was actually a pretty positive reaction.” Teamster sanitation and United Parcel Service workers also refused to service the hotel during the strike. Corral reported seeing the hotel’s director and assistant director hauling garbage out during the World Cup. “It felt so rewarding,” said Desmarais. “Yeah, you have to get your hands dirty and not just do paperwork. I think it gave them a real experience of what we have to deal with.” Corral said community solidarity was key in getting Hilton to concede. Strikers’ church groups joined the picket line. So did several Seattle elected officials and even some hotel guests. Guests also brought workers donuts, contributed to the strike fund, and left Google reviews urging hotel management to “come to the table” and “sign the contract already.” One temp worker walked off the job after only an hour to join the picket line. Corral said such displays of solidarity made workers “more motivated to keep on.” Many workers worried about money, the future of their jobs, and their families while on strike. But when someone was scared or upset, there was always another worker to help uplift them, said Corral: “We’re like family.” This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.author: Green Mountain DSA
articles.content: HELP SHAPE OUR NEXT YEAR: ANNUAL CONVENTION, SUNDAY, NOVEMBER 15 Green Mountain DSA’s annual convention is Sunday, November 15, at the Socialist Labor Party Hall, 46 Granite Street in Barre. We’ll begin around 11 a.m. and continue through the late afternoon. At convention, we’ll elect chapter officers and committee chairs and consider resolutions and bylaws amendments that will shape our work in the coming year. We strongly encourage members to attend in person. It’s a chance to meet comrades from across Vermont and have a say in what we take on together. A virtual option is also available. Register in advance and find convention details. The convention page also has the form for nominating chapter officers and committee chairs. FIVE GREEN MOUNTAIN DSA ENDORSEES HEADED TO MONTPELIER AND A BIG NIGHT FOR DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS NATIONWIDE While we’re disappointed that Phil Scott won a sixth term as governor, Tuesday was a night where working people made it clear that it's time for change here in Vermont and nationwide. Working Vermonters still need housing we can afford, healthcare we can count on, and public services that meet our needs. We’ll keep organizing for those priorities in our communities and at the State House. We’re proud to celebrate five of our six endorsed candidates winning seats in the Vermont General Assembly. Tanya Vyhovsky won reelection to the Vermont Senate, and Trang Do, Jeffrey Peterson, Matt Gile, and Adam Franz won seats in the Vermont House. We also thank Alexander Bobella and the volunteers who worked on his Senate campaign laying the groundwork for a socialist flip in that county in the future. Thank you to everyone who knocked doors, talked to neighbors, and helped get out the vote. When the legislature convenes, those same relationships will matter as we organize around the issues we heard about on the doorstep. Across the country, voters delivered a blow to the Trump administration by taking both chambers of Congress out of Republican hands. DSA candidates also won races for Congress, state legislatures, and local office. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib won reelection to the U.S. House. They’ll be joined by Darializa Avila Chevalier, Claire Valdez, Donavan McKinney, Melat Kiros, Chris Rabb, and Angela Gonzales-Torres. These wins give working people more allies in office as we organize for universal healthcare, stronger labor rights, and an end to ICE. See DSA’s nationwide election results . TAX THE RICH: MONTPELIER AND WINOOSKI CANVASSES FOR TOWN MEETING DAY 2027 BALLOT QUESTIONS Our Tax the Rich campaign is calling on Vermont lawmakers to raise taxes on the richest 5 percent, tax the proceeds of wealth, and use the revenue to make healthcare affordable and accessible. In Montpelier and Winooski, the campaign has been working to put advisory questions on the Town Meeting Day 2027 ballots so residents can weigh in. Sign up to help us collect signatures on our Tax the Rich ballot petitions (advisory questions for the Town Meeting Day Ballot in Montpelier and Winooski)! Winooski -- Saturday, November 14, 1-3 p.m. @ 53 Lafountain St. Montpelier -- Sunday, November 22, 10 a.m. to 12 p.m. @ Montpelier High School Winooski -- Sunday, November 29, 1-3 p.m. @ 53 Lafountain St. Sign up GREEN MOUNTAIN DSA MONTH IN REVIEW In the final weeks before Election Day, members knocked doors for our endorsed candidates, including Adam Franz in Burlington and Alexander Bobella in Franklin County. Thank you to everyone who spent part of an October evening or weekend out talking with neighbors. On October 26, members joined the May Day Strong coalition at Burlington City Hall to oppose the Burlington Forward resolution and its push for more policing. Earlier in the month, we stood with UVM Staff United at its October 20 bargaining kickoff outside Howe Library. University staff are fighting for a fair contract, and we were glad to show that their fight has support beyond campus. Members also worked with comrades in Southern Vermont to build a local presence, including a general interest meeting in Brattleboro, and prepared proposals for our November convention. We closed out the month with a group outing to The Rocky Horror Picture Show . After weeks of canvassing and meetings, it was good to spend an evening together at the movies. WE’RE BUILDING A FAMILY-FRIENDLY GMDSA Green Mountain Democratic Socialists of America is working towards making our organization more accessible to parents and guardians. In August we were approved to receive a chapter Growth and Development grant from DSA national to help with this effort, among other priorities. You can help us by letting us know if you would benefit from childcare being offered at our general meetings. Please fill out our Childcare Needs Survey: https://forms.gle/6Mq1KHWGrc3QgLGv8 UPCOMING GREEN MOUNTAIN DSA MEETINGS Our Labor Committee meets on the second Monday of every month at 6:00pm on Zoom , including Monday Nov 09 . Talk about your job and learn about shop-floor organizing from peers at Workers' Circle (co-hosted with the Green Mountain IWW) on the second and fourth Wednesdays of each month, including Wednesday Nov 11 at 6:00pm at Migrant Justice (179 S. Winooski Ave in Burlington). Our annual chapter convention is Sunday Nov 15 at the Socialist Labor Party Hall (46 Granite St in Barre). This is the most important GMDSA event of the year! The convention will open promptly at 11:00am. Members: check your DSA email for further communication about submitting bylaws amendments and resolutions for debate at convention and to register. Add our Google Calendar - Check out our website - Follow us on Instagram , Threads , Facebook , and BlueSky IMPORTANT DATES THIS YEAR Wednesday, November 11, 6 p.m. ET | Workers’ Circle. Join Green Mountain DSA and the Green Mountain IWW at Migrant Justice, 179 South Winooski Avenue in Burlington, to talk with other workers about organizing on the job.
