articles.title: Did Moderate Democrats Really Outperform the Left? No.
articles.author: Matt Bruenig
articles.content: Democrats did well in the 2026 midterm elections. According to the current tally, they gained forty-one House seats , eight Senate seats , and five governorships . Democratic candidates of all types had success, making it difficult to easily point the finger at this or that faction for blowing the election. This has generated some frustration among factional partisans because such partisans are heavily invested in the idea that their style of politics is electorally superior to the politics of other factions. They can’t point to winners and losers to support their positions because, in this election, everyone was a winner. So they are forced to make their case by analyzing margins of victory, which is hard to do well and full of uncertainty even when it is done well. In this piece, I walk through various approaches to quantifying candidate-specific performance to provide a sort of primer on how to think about this and successfully navigate the deluge of election pseudo-statistics. I. Raw Vote Share The most obvious, though naive, way to distinguish between winners is to look at their raw vote share. If one Democratic candidate won 51 percent of the votes cast in their race and another won 70 percent of the votes cast in their race, then, at a glance, it seems like you could say that the 70-percent candidate performed better than the 51-percent candidate. Certainly the 70-percent candidate did better, but this is not the same thing as performing better. When pundits talk about performance, they are trying to isolate the effect the candidate’s own characteristics had on the election results. Raw vote shares do not do this because raw vote shares reflect other factors as well, including the underlying tendencies of the voters in that area. In other words, it’s possible that the 70-percent district leans more Democratic, and the 51-percent candidate would have also gotten 70 percent in that district. II. Expected Vote Share To isolate the candidate-specific effects, you have to establish some kind of baseline figure for what the election results would have been in a hypothetical version of the race where the candidate was a “generic” Democrat. The difference between the actual results and these “expected” results is then assumed to reflect the unique characteristics of the candidate. This is not an easy thing to do, and most of the efforts I see in the discourse are ridiculous. A. Uniform Swing as Expected Vote Share The most common approach to quantifying expected vote share is to determine how vote shares changed nationally from the prior election and then assign that change uniformly across every voting area in the country. This is what Kevin Deluca did in the following graph. It may look sophisticated, but, as the caption explains, all Deluca did was go through each of the twelve states and add 7.5 points to Kamala Harris’s 2024 presidential result in that state. This is his entire model for expected vote share. The difference between this expected vote and the actual vote is then used to declare underperformers and overperformers. The simplicity of this model is very charming and no doubt explains why I see it more than any other: anyone who can add and subtract is capable of running the model. But does it really make sense to suppose that, if you ran a generic Democrat in every Senate race in the country, each of them would have received a Harris+7.5 vote share? Even if one were to suppose that all of the noncandidate differences between these states and races could be fully captured by Harris’s 2024 presidential result, why would equal performances by generic Senate candidates show up as equal changes in percentage points? Wouldn’t it make more sense for equal performances to show up as equal changes in percent of the 2024 non-Democratic share that was converted to the 2026 Democratic share? To see what I mean, imagine two House districts, one where Harris got 80 percent of the vote in 2024 and another where Harris got 20 percent of the vote in 2024. If you put equally-performing generic Democrats in those districts, what would you expect the result to be? The uniform-swing approach says that we should expect them to add the same number of percentage points. So, for example, we should expect the 80-percent district to become a 90-percent district and the 20-percent district to become a 30-percent district. In this scenario, both districts moved equally by 10 points. But to move 10 points in the 80-percent district, you have to persuade 50 percent of the non-Democratic voters. Moving 10 points in the 20-percent district only requires persuading 12.5 percent of the non-Democratic voters. Why would we expect one generic Democrat to be four times as persuasive as another generic Democrat? How is that equal performance? The premise of the uniform-swing model, which is that equal performance equates to equal percentage points, is nonsensical on its face. Clearly, the number of points an equal performer can move will vary state to state and district to district by the share of the electorate that is even capable of being moved. Simple linear regressions using the House and Senate results provide some empirical support for this point. There are at least two other big problems with this approach to modeling expected vote share. First, a uniform vote swing would make sense only if you were modeling generic Democrat versus generic Republican. But these Senate races do not have generic Republicans in them. Maine’s Troy Jackson ran against a thirty-year incumbent in Susan Collins, while Texas’s James Talarico ran against a scandal-plagued nonincumbent in Ken Paxton. The difference between actual vote share and expected vote share would capture the combined candidate effects of both the Democratic candidate and the Republican candidate. So, for instance, if Troy Jackson runs 2 points behind the uniform-swing expected vote share, that could be because he has negative candidate effects, because Collins has positive candidate effects, or because of some combination of the two. Likewise, if Talarico runs 2 points ahead of the generic-versus-generic expected vote share, that could be because he has positive candidate effects or because Paxton has negative candidate effects. By construction, the uniform-swing approach assumes that the relative overperformance or underperformance of Republican candidates is uniformly zero. Second, different districts have different demographic compositions, which should generate different swings even with equally-performing generic Democrats. For example, here’s what percent of each racial group voted for the Dems nationally in 2024 and 2026. As we can see, the vote swing varies by racial group. Given this variation, the only way equally-performing generic Democrats would generate uniform vote swings in every voting district is if every voting district had the same racial demographics. They don’t. Race is the most obvious example, but other demographic variables like income and education vary across districts and also drive differential vote swings separate from anything having to do with candidate effects. B. Overlapping Elections as Expected Vote Share The second most common approach to quantifying expected vote share is to compare a specific Democratic candidate’s vote share to the vote share of other Democratic candidates running for other positions within the same voting area. So, for instance, you might compare how one statewide candidate did to how other statewide candidates in that same state did. This approach avoids some of the problems of the uniform-swing approach. It does not require us to clumsily extrapolate from prior election results. By construction, it controls for demographics and other sorts of variation between different groups of voters because it compares how different candidates did among the exact same voters in the same year. No longer are we stuck having to wonder whether Michigan 2024 is comparable to Michigan 2026 or whether Michigan 2026 is comparable to Texas 2026. Instead, this approach just compares Michigan 2026 to Michigan 2026. But this overlapping-elections approach still has some of the same problems as the uniform-swing approach and some unique problems of its own. Like the uniform-swing approach, the overlapping-elections approach effectively assumes that Republican candidates never underperform or overperform. But this is obviously untrue. In Texas, Senator-elect Talarico (Dem) received 55.1 percent of the vote while Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa (Dem) received 52.8 percent of the vote. The overlapping-elections approach would say that Talarico overperformed by 2.3 points, or, alternatively, that Hinojosa underperformed by 2.3 points. But these numbers don’t allow us to reach any such conclusion. After all, another explanation would be that Talarico and Hinojosa performed exactly the same while Talarico’s opponent, the scandal-plagued first-time Senate candidate Ken Paxton, underperformed by 1.15 points and Hinojosa’s opponent, the twelve-year incumbent Greg Abbott, overperformed by 1.15 points. The overlapping-elections approach is also unable to determine the absolute quality of the candidates in a given geography, only their relative positions to one another (if that). The uniform-swing approach presumably uses national averages on the theory that a large sample across many geographies provides a more reliable indicator of what the average candidate quality is. But if your dataset only includes a handful of overlapping races, it’s quite possible that a disproportionate share of the candidates in your dataset (even, potentially, all of the candidates in your dataset) are underperformers or overperformers. A senator who runs slightly above a governor or the combined House vote could be an overperformer, but they might also be an underperformer surrounded by even greater underperformers. This approach cannot distinguish between the two. Another unique problem with the overlapping-elections approach is that it assumes that the only reason a voter would split their ticket — e.g., vote for a Democrat for senator and then a Republican for governor or House of Representatives — is because of the different characteristics of the candidates running in the various races. But this is not true. A voter might also split their ticket because of differences in the powers of the various offices they are voting on. A voter who typically supports Republicans but dislikes Donald Trump and wants to rein in his power may support a Republican for governor while supporting a Democrat for the House. That same lean-Republican voter, while supporting a Democrat for the House, might support a Republican for the Senate, given that senators serve six-year terms while all House representatives come up for reelection again in 2028. Even if only a small percentage of voters think in this (quite rational) ticket-splitting way, it’s enough to completely swamp most of the point differences we see in these overlapping-election results, especially when you add in the other problems identified above. C. Regression Models One of the least common approaches to quantifying expected vote share is also the most sophisticated: regression models. Rather than assuming a uniform swing or looking at overlapping elections, throw a variety of variables into a model that spits out an expected vote share for each geography. The difference between what the model outputs and the actual vote share is then presumed to be driven by candidate effects. As far as I know, the two main sources for this approach are Split Ticket , which is now at The Argument , and Strength in Numbers led by G. Elliot Morris. In this election, the Strength in Numbers approach showed no real difference between the various ideological groupings of House candidates. If anything, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) candidates overperformed the average Democrat. Split Ticket, which uses a different regression model, reached a similar result, with only the Blue Dogs and Justice Democrat candidates posting performance results (slightly) distinguishable from zero. The Economist also published the results of a model it apparently put together for the election. According to this model and its candidate groupings, moderates outperformed expectation by less than 1 point while progressives underperformed expectation by the same amount. The main problem with this modeling approach is just that it is not totally clear what variables should be included in the models. This is why they all differ from one another. Another problem, which plagues all of these expected-vote approaches, is that not all candidate effects are related to ideology. Candidates might do better or worse because of their identity, e.g., being a Muslim. They might do better or worse because of their personality, e.g., being charismatic or not. Indeed, as we can see in the scatterplots above, the differences between candidates in each bucket far exceed the average differences between the candidate buckets. This problem is especially relevant when it comes to candidate selection, e.g., when voting in a Democratic primary, because it suggests that the nonideological aspects of candidates completely swamp the ideological aspects. Arguably, these problems could be waved away if the various models all reached similar conclusions about candidate quality and did so at margins too large to plausibly deny. When it comes to the progressive-versus-moderates question, these three regression models do basically reach similar conclusions, which is a null conclusion. What departures we see from null in some of the models on some of the candidate groupings are so small that any grains of salt completely eradicate them. III. Where That Leaves Us Obviously, most discourse participants don’t care about any of this and are happy to move around whatever chart they see that shows that science proves their politics is the best politics. But among pro-moderate pundits who do care at least some about maintaining a defensible argument on the merits, what I have seen lately is a proposal of sorts in which pro-progressive pundits agree that moderates do better than progressives in exchange for pro-moderate pundits agreeing that the gap is very small. Both Jonathan Chait and Matt Yglesias have gone this route after the election. In more recent exchanges I’ve had with Yglesias, he seems to retreat a bit further toward acknowledging that the moderate advantage can’t be reliably demonstrated in the data but that it rests on strong theoretical foundations. The problem with these strategic retreats is that the difference between zero and nearly-zero is not going to be big enough to convince anyone to abandon policy initiatives that they think are important, especially given that policy popularity changes over time in part due to the advocacy of policy partisans. If the current electoral penalty of advocating single-payer health care over expanding Obamacare subsidies is 1 point or less, it would be crazy for someone who believes single-payer health care would dramatically improve society to give it up, especially when the alternative of attempting to persuade some voters to change their minds on that, which includes running candidates who argue for it, also exists. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Progressive Activists Win Elections
articles.author: Michael Albert
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Electoral effort powerfully trounced Trumpism. Not to death, but getting closer. Some election postmortem prescriptions inspire. Some disturb. Which is which? Large sectors of America want serious change. Perched a bit behind them, many other Americans are wavering. And next on the involvement spectrum, quite a few MAGA members are seriously shook up. What can now sustain the gains to go further? As with most social issues and possibilities, there are better and worse answers. Can we at least identify a dividing line? Can we even agree on what makes activist choices better or worse? Can we describe some specific choices of each sort? If so, perhaps we can use such criteria in context of our situations and preferences to choose tasks wisely. To see a dividing line is easy enough. Good choices communicate and act in ways that reveal the possibility of worthy sustainable change. They might bring MAGA-leaning and other system defenders out of system defense. They might bring cynics away from passivity. They might bring anger toward advocating change and bring inactive toward collective activity. In contrast, choices that urge, entice, or even unintentionally move people toward cynical system defense will be negative. Think of the population as people with diverse beliefs and habits that propel or inhibit their seeking new social relations. With that image in mind, good post-election choices will promote, attract, and welcome folks from various positions on the “involvement spectrum” toward the progressive, active end. Harmful post-election words and actions will entrench people far from activism or even move them into aggressive defense of existing relations. Is this explanatory picture too damn simple to help us? It doesn’t touch every base. It isn’t precise. But I think it’s more complex than it at first appears. For example, if your post-election words and deeds tend to move people out of MAGA is that more or less valuable than if your words and deeds move people from passivity toward progressive involvement, or from being somewhat active toward being more active? It depends not only on how much people moved, but are we talking about immediate or longer-term impact? Still, a shift toward progressive change from every position on the involvement spectrum will certainly be positive. Likewise, to shift people toward passivity or even toward defending or worsening the system from every position will certainly be negative. But the devil is in the details. Related: Beyond the Blue Wave: Why Winning Elections Isn't Enough Will any specific choice slide people one way or the other along the involvement spectrum? And of all the possible choices that push positively, which should we aid? Do we ask that question? Do we orient ourselves in part in light of our answers? Can we even assess what specifically moves people toward the progressive or even the radical or revolutionary end of the involvement spectrum? Or assess what instead moves people toward the reactionary, system-defending, cynically a-political, passive or even submissive end of the involvement spectrum? And to complicate assessments, don’t some choices move some people one way but other people the opposite way? We won’t all suddenly agree on the extent of the push-toward-activism or push away from activism effects of different choices on different people. So is one choice certainly right with all other choices certainly wrong? My first point is that no one should say to other activists do it my way or you are part of the problem. Do it my way or you are my enemy. That is a sectarian path that would squander current momentum. To instead respectfully consider and assess contending possibilities would likely be far more productive. But in that case, what options do people currently propose? Hold Trump and his sycophants accountable with public investigations, impeachments, and prosecutions. Prepare to win bigger ballot box gains in 2028 by working electorally with the Democratic Party as a whole or with particular preferred candidates even while opposing others. Urge, demand and organize to win universal free health care, an end to ICE and to the war with Iran and to weapons sales to Israel, restore public education, protect sexual and social diversity, restore cancelled government agencies, prosecute corruption, terminate tariff idiocy, reduce prices, lift low incomes, and enact a national wealth tax plus draconian consequences for trying to flee it. Use diverse words and tactics to accomplish each. Promote, urge, and organize new workplace, campus, and community organizations and grow existing ones. And develop and spread shared social vision, strategy, and program to orient institutional renovations and inspire sustained struggle beyond 2028. All four types of activity and their many possible diverse tactics and messages can slide involved activists, beneficiaries of the efforts, and even viewers of the efforts along the involvement spectrum. Done dismissively the drift could generate antagonism and even hostility more than it generates support. Done in ways that hear, welcome, and empower whoever the efforts encounter, the drift could be overwhelmingly positive. The point is that the consequences of what we choose to do can slide those immediately involved, those affected, and those who just hear or watch what follows. All matter. Related: Upsurges Bubble Around the Globe but Will it Evolve into Effective Change? So what should an organization or even just an individual choose to do? How should we decide our personal or organizational agendas? Again there is no one right answer nor even a single right way to think about choosing among possibilities. Some people might best do elements of 1 above, or of 2, 3, or 4, or even of a combination of them and might act with one or another set of tactics. One general consideration might be do different paths require more or less time from participants, duration of involvement, scale of commitment, knowledge of circumstances, and past organizing experience. Where does an organization or where do we as individuals sit on the experience/knowledge/available time spectrum? Are we just getting started in social change or are we quite experienced? How much time can we commit? What the hell am I getting at? As choices of sort 1 through 4 and perhaps others too unfold and seek support some projects will especially welcome and benefit from newcomers but will be less good at utilizing the accumulated lessons or longer time commitments that other potential participants have to give. In contrast, other projects may need greater prior experience and time commitments and more effectively utilize it. Surely in coming months everyone who wants to go forward and not backward will face challenging choices. Suppose we ask not what we like the looks of. Not, where will more people who we know and like be involved. Not, what will be most fun or easiest for us. And not even what we think is the most important task to now accomplish. Suppose we or our organizations instead ask where can we help in a sustained way where we can best utilize whatever learned abilities and other knowledge and time we have and also not occupy a spot that someone with less experience, knowledge and time could do just as well and benefit more from? In other words first we might figure out where we are needed and would not be redundant. And then we might consult a list of what seems most important to get done and ask of all the tasks on that list what could we engage with effectively and sustainably, which would be most sensible to help accomplish. That is one approach individuals and organizations could use to decide, though of course to pursue any approach inflexibly could easily do more harm than good. Specifics are crucial. Exceptions matter. But, nonetheless, let’s very briefly reconsider the four avenues of possible activity mentioned earlier in light of the need to slide people positively along the involvement spectrum and the advisability to apportion our energies there. Related: Trump Needs “Good Americans” to Look the Other Way Type one activity is to hold Trump and his sycophants accountable with public investigations, impeachments, and prosecutions. While this is mostly activity for elected officials, others might organize, write and speak about the need for it, or might report on it and urge it. The potentially positive aspect is that the type 1 choices can advance the concept of accountability and reduce prospects of these vile characters doing further damage. But negatively, type 1 pursuits might distract Congress and others from working on positive policies and may highlight bad individuals but not bad institutions. Type one choices may highlight “low-bar” changes to get rid of grotesque criminality but ignore more substantive policy much less structural possibilities. At its worst, type 1 activity might complain about Hegseth having weakened America (which is arguably the only positive accomplishment of Trump’s whole tenure) but not address the perversity of war itself. To highlight to punish criminality might say nothing about what ought to characterize a worthy cabinet member or President while it emphasizes only that a Secretary of War should not be a bigoted, violence-worshipping psychopath and a Secretary of Health and Human Services should not be a pseudo scientific self-seeking anti-health nut. Such work might positively affect some on the involvement spectrum, but it could also bore and make cynical many others. It may be the best that activists can reasonably hope for from some elected officials so it is better than if they do nothing especially if some activists pressure outcomes so as to accentuate positive and diminish negative effects. Still, for the most part this isn’t a path likely to effectively utilize experienced radical energies—with perhaps one possible exception. Unlike dumping the likes of Hegseth, etc., work to remove Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries from Democratic Party leadership, especially if it clearly indicates what it would take for new candidates to be worth supporting, could push beyond castigating personal failings to help define and pursue positive policy and structural gains. Type two activity is to win still bigger ballot box gains in 2028 by working with the Democratic Party as a whole or with particular preferred candidates while opposing others. This could certainly welcome new people into outreach activity while simultaneously preparing to win new gains. It could arouse hope and attention and involve new recruits rather like the midterms did only much more so. But how to do this constructively is another matter. Supposing one’s overall goal is to improve conditions for current victims of injustice at home and abroad, if type 2 activity were to melt into compliant Democratic Party allegiance it could limit positive prospects and be unlikely to permanently shift many people on the involvement spectrum other than, perhaps, toward cynicism. On the other hand, to build support for particular demonstrably progressive candidates and especially to build grassroots mechanisms to inform and pressure such candidates and later office holders to radically address public needs could be part of positively shifting popular commitments and desires. How words and actions communicate, as well as the votes they garner, would matter. Type 3 activity is to organize to win universal free health care, an end to ICE, an end to the Iran war, the Israeli/U.S. genocide terminated, public education restored, sexual and social diversity defended, cancelled departments and programs brought back better, corruption prosecuted, tariff idiocy terminated, price controls enacted, low incomes raised, a national wealth tax with draconian consequences for trying to flee it, and so on. These choices can improve people’s lives especially if they are pursued creatively and not solely as ends but also as means to produce growing desires and then pursue them. They can slide people leftward on the involvement spectrum and elevate reasoned hope. Type 3 activity would then have no negatives unless it’s rhetoric and tactics, were to repel rather than attract public support. Fighting for something good by using words and acts that induce fear of change or that castigate and shame potential new people rather than hear and reach out to them can slide involvement in the wrong direction and also provoke preventable repression, so to carefully avoid such debits matters. Type 4 activity is to build activism and consciousness able to inspire on-going struggle beyond 2028 by developing new workplace, campus, and community organizations and movements, growing existing ones, and especially developing and advocating shared social vision, strategy, and program able to orient future institutional renovation. To try to accomplish all that without simultaneous efforts to grow popular support would ultimately fail to deliver. Then again so would to only slide people along the involvement spectrum without having developed means and aims that growing numbers of motivated people could pursue. Strategy has many facets. Being strategic is necessary to keep momentum building. Related: From the New Left to Trump: Why Movements of the 1960s Failed to Build Lasting Power If the above suggestions have merit, what might DSA, for example, choose to do to slide public consciousness along the involvement spectrum and to prod and pursue sustainable movement growth? Where might DSA-level organization and energy be most effectively applied? Different people will likely see this differently but I would suggest least attention and perhaps even none should go directly to type 1 activity. If needed, some attention should go to type 2 activity while carefully retaining an external independent identity and recognizing that electoral victories in 2028 may not require very much DSA time and creativity supposing massive electoral participation rises from previously less experienced people via effective candidate outreach. In that case, considerable DSA level organization, thought, and organizing might better go to type 3 struggles and especially to type 4 vision, strategy, and organization building. So we have lots of if/then formulations. Can we say anything definitive? Perhaps that while paralysis due to excessive analysis is possible, a shortage of effective analysis pretty much guarantees that we will squander energetic effort in unproductive or even destructive pursuits. To perceive and take account of local contexts and especially wide consequences is an essential part of doing good work. Z Network

articles.title: Transnational Prosecutions
articles.author: Ann Garrison
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. At 7 pm on Saturday, November 7th, ICE agents appeared at the Plymouth Correctional Facility in Plymouth, Massachusetts, and handcuffed prisoner Jean Léonard Teganya. No one knew of his whereabouts after that until Monday, November 9 when his family in Canada and the US learned that he was in Kigali, Rwanda, deported even though his appeal of a deportation order was still pending. The essentials of his case are, as I have described them here before: A Rwandan refugee of Hutu ethnicity is charged with genocide crime decades after the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. Witnesses in Rwanda make accusations that they have for some reason kept to themselves for decades. No hard evidence is produced. A jury convicts the accused because they are a Hutu and all Hutus are assumed to be guilty of genocide crime. Although the jurors may give other reasons, they believe that Hutus were the only killers in Rwanda in 1994, that they massacred 800,000 or a million innocent Tutsis and “moderate Hutus,” so this Hutu defendant must be guilty like all the others. Related: Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize and the Dark Legacy of the Rwanda Tribunal The accused then serves time in an American prison for hiding his guilt of genocide crime on his immigration papers. Upon release, he or she faces deportation to stand trial for genocide crimes in Rwanda, where they are convicted and sentenced, usually to life in prison. The Rwandan press is all controlled by President Paul Kagame’s totalitarian regime. The central narrative that it constantly repeats is that only Hutus committed crimes during Rwanda’s 1990-1994 war and during the massacres of its final 100 days. This narrative is even legally enforced; anyone who differs can go to prison for the crime of “genocide denial” in Rwanda. When social scientists Christian Davenport and Allan Stamm went to Rwanda to study the war and genocide, they quickly concluded that something was wrong with the story because everyone recited it as though by rote, exactly the same, without variation, as Allen Stam explained in his University of Michigan lecture “ Understanding the Rwandan Genocide .” This story of Tutsi innocence and Hutu guilt was spread worldwide by the hugely persuasive Hollywood movie Hotel Rwanda. It was institutionalized by the International Criminal Tribunal on Rwanda, which never indicted a single Tutsi, including the one who most deserved indictment—then General, now President Paul Kagame. Kagame’s own Chief of Staff, General Kayumba Nyamwasa told the BBC, in Rwanda’s Untold Story , that he ordered soldiers to assassinate Rwandan President Juvenal Habyarimana and Burundian President Cyprien Ntaryamira by shooting their plane out of the sky over Kigali on April 6, 1994. Those assassinations panicked the population, including the million IDPs in camps encircling Kigali after four years of civil war, and triggered the infamous massacres known as the genocide. Related: Ethiopia vs. Eritrea: A New War Could Send Oil and Gas Prices Soaring It has also been proven, by author Judi Rever and others, that as many or more Hutus died during the war and genocide, and that Kagame’s troops had infiltrated the Interahamwe, the government’s youth militia, and then egged them on during the killing to engineer the genocide that later gave him a specious excuse to rule. After seizing power, Kagame claimed to be the hero who had ended the genocide when in fact he started it, and Western leaders, most notably Bill Cinton and Tony Blair, reinforce that claim to this day. In 2009, in a particularly Orwellian moment, Bill Clinton presented Kagame with a Gloobal Citizen Award for Leadership in Public Service. Even this, however, is not enough. In order to remain in power, the Kagame regime must make sure that Rwandans in diaspora are constantly afraid, fearful of speaking out against the Rwandan government’s domestic repression or its 30+ years of war and resource plunder in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. These prosecutions and deportations are central to maintaining that climate of fear and Western governments, including the US, have been more than willing to collaborate. The mining and industrial interests they represent have benefited hugely from the resource plunder, all according to plan, and as documented in decades of UN reports . No innocence presumed As soon as Jean Léonard Teganya arrived in Rwanda, Kagame’s most prominent media vehicle, the New Times of Rwanda, ran the headline “ Minister Bizimana on US-deported Teganya: 'He was a cruel killer and rapist'. ” Jean-Damascène Bizimana is, laughably, the Minister of National Unity and Civic Engagement. Why bother to stage a trial without presumed innocence, the first principle of criminal law? Because for years, the West has expected Kagame to stage such trials just as he stages elections, the last of which he “won” by 98.2% . Related: Trump Amps Up Anti-Ilhan, anti-Somali Hysteria On November 10, Aljazeera published what they call an “Explainer” headlined “ Who is Jean Léonard Teganya, deported by US over Rwanda genocide claims? ” It said: "He [Jean Léonard] applied for asylum in Canada, but his application was rejected in 2002 and again in 2012. The Canadian authorities’ decision, as described in the US appeal judgement, was based on the conclusion that he would not have survived in Rwanda in 1994 if he had not been perceived as sharing the intention to kill Tutsi and moderate Hutu.” This is more of the non-stop illogic of Rwanda’s totalitarian narrative, which most of the world has accepted since 1994. By that measure, every single Hutu who survived the genocide must have “shared the intent to kill Tutsi and moderate Hutu.” How then could any of the famous “moderate Hutu” have survived? Next in the Dock: Eric Tabaro Nshimiye Any Rwandan who dares to testify on behalf of another in one of these trials is likely to find themselves accused, indicted, prosecuted, deported, and imprisoned in time as well. Eric Tabaro Nshimiye testified on behalf of Jean Léonard Teganya in 2019, and on October 26, 2016, a jury found him guilty of lying on his immigration papers and lying on behalf of Jean Léonard. Eric and Jean Léonard were both medical students at the University of Rwanda’s teaching hospital in Butare in 1994, at the time of the massacres. Seven years ago, after Eric testified on Jean Léonard’s behalf, a criminal defense attorney urged him to leave the US, to find another home and establish another identity wherever he could because there was no doubt that he would be next and no chance he would receive a fair trial. But Eric didn’t run. He has work, family, faith, and community here. For more than two decades, he has worked for Goodyear Tire and Rubber as an electrical engineer while living in Lake Township, in the Uniontown, Ohio area. In March 2024, he was arrested and charged with crimes like those Jean Léonard and so many others have been charged with. In the Ohio District Court, seventy friends and family members, including even his dentist, submitted statements to say that he is a devoted husband and father and an upstanding, engaged member of his community and church. Friends and family traveled from all over the US and even Canada for his detention hearing in Youngstown. They stood outside with signs reading, “Eric Is a Man of Virtue,” “Eric Is a Man of High Morals,” “Eric Is a Man of Faith,” and more. As reported by the Canton Repository , “they huddled in prayer, hugged, shook hands and shed a few tears.” They have no doubt seen this pattern play out many times before. I traveled to Boston for Eric’s arraignment in federal court, where family filled all the benches in a small courtroom, then offered up the equity in their homes as bail, hoping to secure his release while awaiting trial. Sadly, they failed and on October 26, 2026, Eric was convicted. He now awaits sentencing on January 26 next year. Related: Trump Amps Up Anti-Ilhan, anti-Somali Hysteria In the backdrop of Eric and Jean Léonard’s tragedies is that of political prisoner Victoire Ingabire Umuhoza, who left a very successful, settled life in the Netherlands in 2010 to return to Rwanda and challenge Paul Kagame in that year’s presidential election. She went to prison for the “crime” instead. Perhaps even more importantly, she was convicted of “genocide denial,” of challenging the singular narrative that only Hutus committed crimes during Rwanda’s war and genocide, that only Hutus, and even their children, will pay for them now and forever. She left the Netherlands knowing that she would likely be assassinated or imprisoned but urging her followers to pick up where she left off. Kagame had Victoire arrested again in June 2025, on charges like fomenting civil unrest and encouraging members of her party to read a book on nonviolent protest. The charges have since been enhanced and this time the prosecution is seeking a life sentence. Rwandan political prisoner Victoire Ingabire's case will resume in Kigali on December 8th. The Prosecutor is seeking a life sentence. In a recent letter to her supporters, she wrote: I am in good spirits, but I am also worried for my life. The recent death of government critic Aimable Karasira in a Rwandan prison on the day he was due for release affirms my worries. I wonder whether I will ever see my family again or even speak to my children and grandchildren. But I am grateful for everyone who has spoken out for me and called for my release. Only a little of what happens outside these prison walls reaches me, but I know I have not been forgotten and I am thankful for that. I appeal to all individuals, institutions, and states that believe in democracy to join me in calling for the Rwandan regime to reform - for the greater good of its citizens and the entire region. I believe in a better future for Rwanda, but it cannot be built while independent voices are silenced." Sadly, this persecution feels neither new nor surprising. Despite what the charges state, my crime is being a woman who is not afraid to dream out loud of a better future for Rwanda. My requests to speak to my children have been refused since my arrest in June 2025. I have only occasionally spoken briefly to my gravely ill husband. There are times when prison guards confiscated my documents and those of my lawyers, thereby interfering with our preparations for my defense. I have been prevented from meeting with my co-accused to prepare my defense and barred from attending worship services within the prison, an opportunity granted to the other inmates. I have been a person of deep faith my entire life. In my darkest moments, I draw great strength from my faith. I believe that by taking away even my right to spiritual nourishment during my imprisonment, the regime is trying to break my will. What they don't understand is that when you know your cause is just, nothing can break you. Black Agenda Report

articles.title: Anthropic’s IPO Is a Bid to Manufacture Confidence
articles.author: Clark Randall
articles.content: Anthropic, maker of artificial intelligence software Claude, is going public this Thursday. The initial public offering (IPO) could top the record SpaceX set earlier this year, once a concurrent private stock placement is counted. In February, Anthropic raised capital at a $380 billion valuation, and it is now seeking buy-in at $1.4 trillion. The rise has only been matched by the demand from investors, as Bloomberg reported the IPO road show was oversubscribed by six times the available shares. In other words, institutions will be crowding out individual investors vying for early gains. Anthropic aims to raise $64 billion from the IPO in a nontraditional coming-to-market event. It has already been widely noted how the IPO’s role has changed over the last decade, with the flipping of public and private functions. Previously companies went public when their growth depended on it, raising capital from the public in order to continue expansion. But today, exponential growth takes place across multiple rounds of buy-in for private credit and venture capital (VC) funds. When those investors are ready to sell, the IPO works, in part, as an exit opportunity. Meaning: the people in the know, inside Anthropic, are rushing to market in order to offload their shares at peak value into your hands. Anthropic is aware of the problem with how this looks. For this reason, out of its IPO of 825 million shares, over 800 million (97 percent) are fresh issuance — newly formed slices of the company that dilute previous shareholders’ stock but have the benefit of providing capital upfront to the company. This is not a normal distribution for a large IPO but does mimic the earlier framework of SpaceX — that is, another company that oriented its price and offering around retail interest. Essentially, these companies are duping investors with the facade of fresh issuance as proof of internal confidence, understanding that selling pressure will spike in the months after the firm goes public. Obscure lockup terms mark out twenty-three liquidity events — days when insiders can sell shares — beginning on the first day of trading. Typically, early investors would wait six months to a year before being able to sell. The thinking is presumably the following: increase public confidence by smoothing out the change of hands, in order to avoid a deluge of shares going live at any one time. Forever Young In preparation for going public, Anthropic filed its S-1 prospectus document with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The tech-and-VC All-In Podcast with Chamath Palihapitiya and Jason Calacanis opened its post-S-1 commentary with David Sacks by calling this the greatest wealth-creation event in the history of Silicon Valley. Indeed, more than a thousand Anthropic employees are in line to make $10–$100 million post-IPO. Calacanis followed up by questioning whether this was the “greatest business in the history of capitalism.” Irony aside, I found the comment thought-provoking. Could it be that Anthropic is the greatest misallocation of capital and the greatest company capitalism has ever produced? This is one of an array of dialectics defining the development of American frontier AI labs. Together they merge imagery from utopic and dystopic futures: we are told that these developments will either eliminate half the workforce, or “create more jobs than they destroy”; solve the climate crisis, or burst the environmental constraints of water, electricity, and critical minerals asunder; they’re either a word-order prediction machine, or an army of banal geniuses. We might be either in the first inning or the ninth: Who can tell? The element in common is that few people in the public eye hold any position in between these extremes. Bifurcated opinion is an accumulation mechanism for these companies; the unknown is the elixir of their success. The moment they become a known quantity is the moment when corporate accounting standards mean something. Palihapitiya of All-In demonstrates the value of AI by citing the fact that a company like Microsoft has grown its revenue by two-thirds ($198 billion to $332 billion) in the past four years without increasing its workforce. The company recently sent buyout offers to 60,000 employees: revenue per worker has skyrocketed, and yet it still sees dead weight everywhere. It’s a story seen across the tech industry. Torsten Slok at Apollo recently found that revenue per employee in the sector is up around 40 percent since the 2022 turning point in AI and has flatlined in the S&P’s remaining 493 companies. We can assume 2022 really was the turning point, after ChatGPT was introduced to the public that November. Yet what happened a month earlier was, I’d argue, far more important to Slok’s findings. Elon Musk acquired Twitter in October 2022, and within the week he halved its workforce and issued work-intensity ultimatums to thousands more. A 7,500-person company was reduced to a little over 1,000 staff. On Twitter (soon renamed X) and in the media , most speculated about the collapse of user experience and platform viability. Instead, nothing really changed; vulgar and racist tweets were widespread, explicit usage of the platform proliferated, but if we’re being honest, nothing collapsed in the way we expected. Bluesky, save for a cohort of academics, has not supplanted X as the place where news headlines are disseminated. Slok’s headline read “No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector,” but this fabricated an impact where it was yet to be observed. The tech sector, led by Musk and backed up by the Effective Altruism crew thereafter, slashed employees and found an unfortunate truth about “bullshit jobs” — that millions of prestigious white-collar positions weren’t materially involved in the production process. The apparent productivity gains owed rather less to a revolutionary AI workforce. The Spectacle of an AI Economy As Anthropic comes to market, we might look for insight from Guy Debord’s Society of the Spectacle . A Marxist and prominent figure among the French situationists in the 1960s, Debord saw the circulation of images as a final evolution in the accumulation process. Surplus ultimately finds itself reinvested as signage, representation, and aesthetics as opposed to the productive economy. Leading up to the IPO, Anthropic deployed a yearlong advertising campaign stretching from the Super Bowl to the FIFA World Cup and every major TV event in between. The tagline? “Keep Thinking.” Over a Rolodex of apocalyptic images, the voices of everyday Americans can be heard questioning the future of AI, saying things from “If they end up taking all the jobs, then what does it really mean to work?” to “Could AI help people stop feeling misunderstood?” The images shift from catastrophe to connection, showing mothers holding daughters and whales breaching water. Debord wrote in 1967 that “the spectacle is the nightmare of imprisoned modern society which ultimately expresses nothing more than its desire to sleep. The spectacle is the guardian of sleep.” Essentially, the spectacle exists as a way of whispering to society: keep sleeping. In response, a revolutionary leader like Malcolm X used to warn his audiences that they must wake up and think for themselves — the subtext being that society will dictate what thoughts are permissible, in order to control how they act. The irony today is that capital no longer cares what we think. We are free now, liberated (encouraged even) to think whatever thoughts we’d like. Our aggregated impressions, worries, and conundrums are catalogued and commodified. We can all be communists, socialists, or anti-capitalists at heart; anything, so long as we keep thinking using their models. When we fear that AI means the end of critical thinking, we may be fearing the wrong thing. Claude and ChatGPT are not the end of our capacity to critique or analyze. If anything, the opposite is true: we enter a mind-numbing labyrinth of critical thoughts, questions, and opinions. These are anti-relational machines, not anti-thinking ones. I was on the phone with my dad the other day; how cool is it, he said, that he can put an image of his struggling plants into ChatGPT and get back a protocol for caretaking. I asked, what would you have done before? I’d probably have called my brother, he answered. AI and Big Tech capital integrated the lessons of postmodernist discourse with surprising effectiveness. Back in a 2013 blog post , author and media theorist Nathan Jurgenson called this the “anti-capitalism-capitalism” of Silicon Valley. Thus far, the debates surrounding Anthropic chief Dario Amodei’s obsession with extinction-level AI events have been somewhat surface-deep. Skeptics like Ed Zitron and Steve Eisman of The Big Short believe it’s a smoke screen for regulatory capture by a company with no economic moat around it. Others take it literally. It’s both and it’s neither: it’s the construction of a discursive world, a spectacle, that distracts us from confronting the distributional politics of AI’s advancement. Dual-Zone Economy In 1987, the stock market crashed on Black Monday at the behest of newly automated computer-programmed trading algorithms, which simultaneously sold stocks as they began to fall due to the macro environment. Some of the conditions from back then again seem familiar — what was then a skirmish with Iranian forces is today a full-blown war; again today, the dollar is weakening both nominally and politically, and global energy markets are stressed. Still, after crashing 20 percent, the indexes finished in 1987 slightly higher than they started it. The temperature of the times blew hot and cold. That same year, German automaker BMW introduced “dual-zone automatic climate control” into its premium vehicles. For the first time, the driver could dial the heat up as their passenger turned the air conditioning on. By the turn of the millennium, most models included some iteration of this. Industry commentators at the time dubbed it “the marriage saver.” The same moving car could now hold two divergent conditions. Today Anthropic chief Amodei, fellow AI kingpins like Sam Altman, and newly disgraced former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang are sitting on each other’s laps in the driver’s seat and running it hot, even despite last week’s drawdown. But we’re in the passenger seat, and the data says it’s cold as can be in here. These companies are public or will be public soon; they, more than anything, will decide the fates of our retirement accounts; their collapse would spell a more widespread recession. They expect us to join them for the ride, for the sake of the marriage. And yet the recent US midterms saw forty of forty-one ballots related to data centers reject them by wide margins. Capitalism’s greatest business is, as Karl Marx predicted, birthing its own gravediggers. Deskilled white-collar labor, though highly paid, is learning of its own immateriality. Working-class Americans are saying no to having their communities repurposed for the sake of technological progress. AI’s advancement and its discontents, as a particular technological revolution distinct from others, are setting the stage for a once-in-a-century kind of cross-class, cross-identity, cross-party opposition. articles.title: Is This the End of Pedro Sánchez?
articles.author: Pablo Castaño
articles.content: In recent years, Pedro Sánchez’s Spanish government, formed by his Socialists (PSOE) and the left-wing alliance Sumar, has been a reference point for the global left. Rarely among social democratic politicians, Sánchez has become well-known for his confrontations with Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu, and for his governing coalition’s progressive social and economic policies. However, Spain’s government could soon fall into the hands of a new alliance of the conservative Partido Popular (PP) and the far-right Vox party. At least, this is what almost all polls now suggest, less than two weeks before the general election on November 29. There are many reasons for the electoral weakness of the PSOE and its further-left allies, now grouped in the Frente Amplio alliance. The broad-left government had already lost its majority in parliament in 2023, forcing it to rely on the votes of regionalist parties. But it has also been hit by its own mistakes as well as a ruthless offensive by traditional Spanish elites. Here are six reasons why the snap elections on November 29 could force Sánchez from office. 1. Complicated Parliamentary Arithmetic After the last general election in 2023, Sánchez only remained prime minister thanks to an eclectic coalition of progressive parties and Catalan, Basque, and Galician nationalists, including conservatives. They were united only by fear of a PP-Vox government that would be very hostile to the cultural and national diversity that defines Spain. Because of the tight electoral results in 2023, the current legislative term has been marked by parliamentary instability and by a no-holds-barred war by the Right against a government that it considered illegitimate from the outset due to its reliance on parties who want independence from Spain. That dependence on conservative formations such as Catalonia’s Junts and, to a lesser extent, the Partido Nacionalista Vasco (PNV) has forced the government to lower its ambition regarding some laws and has cost it important votes in Congress, especially on housing issues. The most serious parliamentary defeat came this October, when PP, Vox, and Junts together rejected two emergency decrees on housing tabled by the government following the eviction of an eighty-seven-year-old woman in Madrid and the subsequent massive demonstrations for the right to housing. Much of the mobilization centered on the government’s inability to curb rents. However, Sánchez also called this snap election hoping that the debate on housing would distract attention from the migration crisis in Ceuta. 2. Stormy Relations With Catalan Conservatives Among the numerous parliamentary groups on which the PSOE-Sumar coalition government depended, the one that has set the highest price for its support has been Junts, a Catalan party which supports pro-business economic policies. This party is led from exile by a former president of the Catalan government, Carles Puigdemont, who until last month feared arrest over his role in organizing the unofficial 2017 independence referendum. Following the 2023 general election, Junts set a price on supporting Sánchez’s investiture as head of government. It said it would only vote to keep him prime minister in exchange for an amnesty law that ended the judicial prosecution of Catalan pro-independence leaders. The approval of the amnesty law in 2024 unleashed a nationalist campaign by the Spanish right, which considers the pro-independence supporters “coup plotters.” This conflict, too, fed Spanish nationalist party Vox’s electoral rise. The PSOE lost the support of numerous voters, and the Right exploited to saturation the idea that Sánchez has no principles and is capable of doing anything to stay in power. The Supreme Court, controlled by a judiciary heavily tilted to the right, has battled to prevent the full application of the law, but it has ended up being applied by order of the Constitutional Court. 3. Lawfare and Corruption The justice system has been one of the main arenas of a fierce opposition to Sánchez. Right-wing ideas are clearly overrepresented in the Spanish judiciary: the two conservative judicial associations gather more than 40 percent of judges, while less than 10 percent belong to the only progressive association (the rest are not part of an association or belong to smaller groupings). To this unbalanced picture is added the growing shamelessness of the most reactionary judges in using the justice system for political ends. This is already shown by the judicial harassment against left-wing party Podemos and, more seriously, against Catalan independence supporters. Various conservative judges have initiated proceedings of dubious justification against Sánchez’s brother and wife, confirming, in the eyes of the right-wing electorate, the idea that the Socialist prime minister is surrounded by corruption. The accusation is especially damaging because Sánchez himself reached the head of government in 2018 thanks to a motion of no confidence after the then-ruling PP was convicted in a serious corruption case. Unfounded accusations against Sánchez’s relatives have been mixed with real cases that have contributed to damaging his popularity: his former number two, ex–Minister of Development José Luis Ábalos, has been sentenced to twenty-four years in prison for taking bribes and awarding public contracts for the purchase of masks during the pandemic, and Santos Cerdán, who was also the PSOE’s organizational secretary, is likewise being investigated for corruption. 4. Insufficient Action on Housing and Inflation The PSOE-Sumar coalition government has managed, despite its parliamentary weakness, to approve important measures such as increases in the minimum wage, the expansion of paternity leave, a boost to pension rates, and a law — albeit an insufficient one — to regulate rental prices. These added to the labor reform that has reduced temporary employment and the creation of a minimum living income to fight poverty, both introduced during the previous PSOE-Podemos government (2020–23). In addition, the macroeconomic data is good: Spain has for years been top of the table for GDP growth among the major European economies, and unemployment is at its lowest level since 2008. However, a large part of the working class has seen its standard of living worsen. The minimum wage has risen almost 75 percent since 2018 (from €858 gross to €1,500 per month), but it has not pulled up wages in general: according to the Juan de Mariana Institute , three out of four wage earners earn under twice the minimum. Meanwhile, inflation reached close to 5 percent this October, and food has become 41.5 percent more expensive since 2018. Even more serious is the escalation of rents, rising 43 percent on average in a decade; in large cities, renting an apartment is equivalent to 100 percent of a young person’s income. The housing situation, which is the main problem for Spaniards according to all polls, translates into more than forty evictions per day, despite the fact that Sánchez promised that this parliamentary term would be “the legislature of housing.” The explosion of the housing movement in recent weeks, which has included the first general strike on this issue in the history of Spain, demonstrates the failure of the coalition government in this key area for the Spanish working class. 5. Immigration and the Rise of Vox The worsening of the material living conditions of much of the middle and working classes has opened up space for Vox’s racist messaging, which has only in recent years managed to sink roots among the lower-income electorate. The sudden entry of more than seventy thousand migrants into Ceuta (Spain’s North African enclave) on July 30–31 seemed to confirm Vox’s rhetoric, which warns of a supposed migrant “invasion.” Santiago Abascal’s Vox has turned the rejection of immigration into its absolute priority, with a discourse that connects it with crime, even though the latter has declined while the number of migrant workers has grown. Its radicalism is akin to that of Germany’s ultranationalist Alternative für Deutschland: in 2025, Abascal incited the racist riots in Torre-Pacheco (Murcia), and a spokeswoman advocated the “remigration” of between seven and eight million people, including Spaniards descended from foreigners. As in other European countries, the conservative PP has contributed to normalizing Vox’s discourse, forming governments with it at the regional level (in Spain’s so-called autonomous communities) and hardening its anti-immigration line. Driven by the reactionary wave that began with Donald Trump’s reelection in 2024, Vox is approaching 20 percent in polls, and no one doubts that it will form a coalition government with Alberto Núñez Feijóo’s PP if the results allow it. 6. A Divided and Weak Left Sánchez could reestablish his coalition government in 2023 thanks to the electoral comeback achieved by his PSOE, but also by Sumar , the formation led by Deputy Premier Yolanda Díaz, which scored 12 percent of the vote. Podemos, which split from Sumar, today has only a small parliamentary representation. For several weeks in October, the alternative left starred in a real soap opera about whether it would form a single candidacy. It was even mooted that such a list would be headed by Gabriel Rufián, of Esquerra Republicana de Catalunya (ERC), the most popular politician to the left of the PSOE in all of Spain, despite his pro-independence stance. Finally, a coalition called Frente Amplio was formed, led by former Barcelona Mayor Ada Colau and including fifteen parties. Podemos refused to join the Frente Amplio despite the great similarity between their programs, and now Podemos is polling under 2 percent support. This division has aggravated the disenchantment of the left-wing electorate. It also reduces the chances of a new broad-left majority, since the electoral system penalizes parties with few votes spread across many provinces, such as Frente Amplio and Podemos. Less than two weeks before the elections, Frente Amplio is aiming for 10 percent of the votes, which would give it between fifteen and twenty seats. But if Colau’s candidacy sinks, even if the PSOE has a decent result, there will hardly be a parliamentary majority willing to keep Sánchez as prime minister. Paradoxically, part of his Socialists’ now-scant hopes lie in the good prospects for Euskal Herria Bildu (in the Basque Country), the ERC (Catalonia), and Adelante Andalucía, three left-wing sovereigntist formations that are growing in the polls and would also vote in favor of Sánchez returning as premier. But Nothing Is Set in Stone To these structural factors was added, a few weeks before the elections, a collision between two trains that caused sixty-nine deaths. This was the second high-speed accident in a year, revealing the deplorable state of the country’s railway infrastructure. The disaster prompted the resignation of Transport Minister Óscar Puente, a Sánchez loyalist. In addition, the accident has weakened one of the PSOE’s main lines of argument: the defense of public services against the “chainsaw” of the Spanish far right, which admires the ultra-free-marketeer economic policies of Argentina’s President Javier Milei. At the time of writing, almost all polls show a considerable majority for the right-wing camp, but they also detect a recent rebound by the PSOE. Both the Socialists and the Frente Amplio want to believe in a scenario like 2023, in which the charismatic Sánchez’s effective campaign and fears of the Right ended up mobilizing the broadly left-wing electorate. However, the government parties would today need to recover much more ground during the campaign than they managed in 2023. A long-enduring right-wing campaign to delegitimize the government, Vox’s strength, and the sustained wear and tear of office means that, for now, the most likely outcome is that Spain loses its luster as a model for the Left. EWOC Fundamentals of Workplace Organizing — November Session Do you have problems at your workplace or generally have frustrations with the systems governing your communities? Would you like to learn how to talk to people in order to build collective power? Are you interested in discussing organizing strategies with comrades of various organizing levels? If you said “yes” to any of those questions (or are just a radical person), attend our sessions each Sunday of November 3:00 – 4:30 PM for the EWOC Fundamentals of Workplace Organizing course! Emergency Workplace Organizing Committee (EWOC) is a collaboration between national DSA and the United Electrical, Radio & Machine Workers of America (UE) to organize unorganized workplaces and build a distributed, grassroots organizing program to support workers organizing at the workplace. This training course is meant to help you build your union from the ground up alongside workers in your industry. It doesn’t require an organizing background to understand the material, which covers topics including mapping and charting, building an organizing committee, uniting over common concerns, and how to take action. If you’re interested in becoming any level of organizer for EWOC, this course is mandatory. This course will be in-person, with the group watching the EWOC lectures and the discussion activities occurring at the DSA office (1916 McAllister) . If you can’t make all of the sessions, reach out to san-francisco@workerorganizing.org for accommodations. RSVP here EWOC Fundamentals of Working Organizing: Week #2 Reportback The second week of the four-week EWOC Fundamentals training was focused on 1:1 conversations. We watched a recorded session, led by a worker that organized at a chocolate factory in SF and is now a labor lawyer, and another worker currently organizing at Whole Foods. Organizing conversations, or 1:1s are the moments where an organizer builds trust with a co-worker, brings them into organizing, and moves them to take a concrete action. They are natural, but built around a 6-step framework that EWOC recommends – (1) intro and building trust (2) finding out the issues your co-worker cares about (3) agitating around those issues, (4) building a vision of a future and a Plan To Win, (5) inoculation to prepare them for the boss’s response, and (6) a concrete ask or Calling the Question. The facilitators stressed that these steps should not feel transactional, and may take many conversations. Building trust and often socializing before you organize are great first steps, rather than checking the boxes of these 6 steps or projecting your own issues onto your co-worker. After the recorded session, our discussion placed these 1:1 conversations in the context of labor law. All portions of the conversation are legally protected by the NLRA, but that shouldn’t be our focus. The Plan To Win is workers taking collective action together, not necessarily a just a legally certified NLRB election and a contract. The workers at Whole Foods won their union certification vote, but still don’t have a contract, and that’s an intentional tactic by the boss. Beyond that, many of the labor victories of the last century, going back to the 8hr day and 5 day work week, were won by militant unions and ‘illegal’ strikes before the Labor Peace of the NLRA. We ended the session by pairing up and practicing 1:1s with each other, with feedback on what we can improve. Every conversation in every workplace will be different, but there’s a framework, and it’s a concrete skill that we can build and practice together. The next (and last) session will take place on Sunday, November 22nd at 3PM, hosted at 1916 McAllister and we will cover inoculation against the boss. If you’d like to get involved with the SF local chapter of EWOC, reach out the EWOC local at san-francisco@workerorganizing.org or email labor@dsasf.org . EWOC is a standing topic at meetings of the Labor Working group, which are held every fourth Monday at 7:00pm, both in-person at 1916 McAllister and over Zoom—the next one will be Monday November 16th! Anyone is welcome to attend, and we’re always looking for people interested in workplace lead canvassing, organizer trainings, and volunteer outreach. If you’re interested in organizing your workplace and would like to be connected with an EWOC organizer, fill out the request form here .

articles.title: Young Voters and the 2026 Blue Wave
articles.author: Randy Shaw
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The Power of Ongoing Outreach A big story behind the blue election tsunami was the sharp rise in youth voting. According to a leading source , youth turnout was 27% across the nation. It was 30% in battleground states. It was the best midterm youth turnout since 2018. Voters under 30 favored Democrats by a whopping 35%. In contrast, voters over 45 were almost equally divided. That’s why many believe “ the youth vote was key to Democratic Wins in the Midterms .” This sharp turnout increase among an historically under-performing demographic has been building for years. While youth turnout was driven by factors shared by the overall electorate, it also reflected a sophisticated organizing strategy led by over 50 youth-oriented groups. These groups reached out to young voters’ months before the election. This investment in year-round youth outreach and organizing paid dividends on election turnout. Blue Future played a key coordination and training role in building the capacity of 53 youth-oriented activist groups . Nick Guthman and Morgan Stahr co-founded Blue Future in 2018. The group has worked tirelessly to build a foundation for year-round youth organizing designed to increase youth voting turnout. Related: Jane Kim and Nithya Raman Defy the Democratic Establishment—and Win 8 Years of Work Pays Off Here’s how Blue Future described in October what its financial support for the over fifty youth activist groups is designed to accomplish: “ Young people are bringing their skills, networks, cultural fluency, and leadership to the 2026 midterms. They are building infrastructure, training the next cohort of organizers, and deploying their lived expertise in communities traditional campaigns have overlooked. The field shares a consistent and multi-faceted tactical approach while drawing on the distinct assets each constituency brings — Hmong networks in Wisconsin, working-class leadership in rural North Carolina, college-town relational networks, multigenerational Jewish communities in Florida, climate expertise, and the trusted voices students already rely on for guidance .” The group is bringing the type of sophisticated analysis that groups like the New Georgia Project have used to trigger sustained turnout gains In addition to funneling funds to youth activist groups, Blue Future has an Organize for Democracy program that trains students in organizing, phone banking and leadership development. Students selected for the program across the nation spend five hours a week working on campaigns. Check out the Organizing Testimonials on the group’s website. These students made 1.2 million calls to voters in 2026! Why Year-Round Outreach on Local Issues Matter Blue Future’s strategy confirms what I argue in a recent story I wrote for Social Policy : investing in ongoing organizing is the best strategy for winning elections (See “ Can We Reverse the Decline in Community Organizing? ”). Here’s how Ohio Student Action describes the connection: “ Across the state, our chapters work hard to make the change they want to see in their communities a reality – whether that’s campus reform, local ballot initiatives, or the state budget, OSA is there. Our mission is simple: create an Ohio where students and young people thrive, and fight for a government that saves a seat for us at the table. ” Young people who get involved in community-based political fights are more likely to see the value in voting. And encourage their family and friends to do so. Related: Prop 40 and the Price of Progressive Disunity More Work to Do The estimated national voter turnout was 53%. So a youth turnout of 30% in battleground states shows the need for muchgreater investment in this group. In 1971, the constitutional amendment reducing the eligible voting age from 21 to 18 was signed into law by Richard Nixon. Three-fourths of the states ratified the constitutional amendment in record time. Why the urgency to expand rather than reduce voting rights? The anti-war movement highlighted that people under 21 drafted for the Vietnam War lacked the right to vote. Rather than end the war, the United States lowered the voting age. Instead of relying on foundations or philanthropists, Blue Future has spent years building a small donor list. This is critical for rebuilding the nation’s community organizing infrastructure as well as youth voter turnout. Why did recent U.S. Senate campaigns deluge us with online requests for as little as $3? Small donors add up—if you have a good list. To that end, Blue Future has a nonprofit organization that can receive tax deductible donations for its training and education work. Y ou can donate here . Those under 35 are so directly impacted by government policies that there’s no reason voter turnout should not be higher. Let’s help make that happen for 2028. Beyond Chron
